structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: The preface presents pattern recognition and machine learning as related fields shaped by major advances in Bayesian methods, graphical models, approximate inference, and kernel-based models. It introduces the textbook’s broad audience, prerequisites, self-contained probability coverage, reference policy, and online supplementary resources. It explains the purpose, difficulty grading, solution access, and recommended use of the chapter exercises, and points to a companion practical volume with Matlab software. The remainder acknowledges the many individuals, institutions, publishers, and contributors who supported the book’s writing, production, figures, permissions, and review, concluding with thanks to the author’s wife and the February 2006 date and location.

structure.title: Mathematical notation
structure.summary: The text establishes the book’s mathematical prerequisites and conceptual emphasis, defines its vector, matrix, interval, identity-matrix, functional, asymptotic, expectation, variance, covariance, and data-matrix notation, and then provides the full contents of a pattern-recognition and machine-learning text. The book covers introductory probability, Bayesian reasoning, decision and information theory; probability distributions and nonparametric methods; regression and classification models; neural networks; kernel and sparse-kernel methods; graphical models; mixture models and EM; variational and sampling-based approximate inference; latent-variable and sequential-data models; model combination methods; exercises throughout; and appendices on data sets, probability distributions, and matrix properties.

nodes.title: 1 Introduction
1.1. Example: Polynomial Curve Fitting
nodes.summary: The text introduces foundational pattern-recognition ideas through noisy polynomial regression. It models data generated from sin(2πx), fits polynomials by minimizing squared error, and explains underfitting, overfitting, model selection, test-set generalization, RMS error, coefficient growth, and the beneficial effect of larger data sets. It then presents regularization as coefficient shrinkage controlled by λ, identifies ridge regression and neural-network weight decay, and discusses validation-based complexity selection, maximum likelihood, and Bayesian alternatives. Finally, it motivates probability theory as a framework for uncertainty and begins its development with a two-box fruit-selection example involving random variables and empirical probabilities.

nodes.title: 1.2. Probability Theory
1.2.1 Probability densities
nodes.summary: The text explains Bayes’ theorem through a fruit-box example, distinguishing prior and posterior probabilities and showing how evidence can reverse an initial preference. It defines independence through factorization of joint distributions and then introduces continuous probability densities, including interval probabilities, nonnegativity and normalization, cumulative distribution functions, multivariate densities, probability mass functions, and Jacobian-based transformation under changes of variables. It states that probability sum and product rules and Bayes’ theorem apply to continuous and mixed variables, with an informal interval-partition justification. Finally, it defines expectations as weighted averages for discrete and continuous distributions and begins discussing their approximation from finite samples.

nodes.title: 1.2.2 Expectations and covariances
nodes.summary: The text explains probability densities and their normalization, the treatment of discrete, continuous, and mixed variables, and the sum and product rules with an informal measure-theoretic justification. It then defines expectations as weighted sums, integrals, sample averages, and conditional or partial averages, followed by definitions and interpretations of variance and covariance for scalar and vector random variables, including the fact that independent variables have zero covariance.

nodes.title: 1.2.3 Bayesian probabilities
nodes.summary: The text introduces Bayesian probability as a general framework for quantifying and updating uncertainty, contrasting it with frequentist probability based on repeatable-event frequencies. It motivates probability as rational belief consistent with common-sense axioms, discusses historical contributors and biographies of Bayes and Laplace, and develops Bayes’ theorem for updating uncertainty about model parameters using priors, likelihoods, and posteriors. It compares Bayesian inference with maximum likelihood, bootstrap-based frequentist error assessment, and the role of prior knowledge, while addressing debates over prior choice and model evaluation. It also reviews the computational development of Bayesian methods, including Monte Carlo and deterministic approximations. Finally, it introduces the Gaussian distribution, gives its density formula, and defines its mean, variance, standard deviation, and precision.

nodes.title: 1.2.4 The Gaussian distribution
nodes.summary: The text discusses computational developments enabling Bayesian inference, then introduces the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions and their normalization, moments, variance, mode, and parameters. It formulates the likelihood of i.i.d. Gaussian data, derives maximum-likelihood estimates for the mean and variance, explains numerical use of log likelihood, and shows that the variance estimate is systematically biased downward, along with its unbiased correction and connection to overfitting. Finally, it revisits polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets with a Gaussian centered on the polynomial prediction and governed by a precision parameter.

nodes.title: 1.2.5 Curve fitting re-visited
nodes.summary: The text explains the small-sample downward bias of maximum-likelihood Gaussian variance estimates, its reduction with increasing data, and its connection to overfitting in complex models. It then reformulates polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets with Gaussian noise around the polynomial prediction. Maximum likelihood produces the usual sum-of-squares objective, estimates the noise precision from residuals, and yields a Gaussian predictive distribution. Adding a Gaussian prior over polynomial coefficients leads to MAP estimation, which is equivalent to regularized least squares with lambda = alpha/beta. The text concludes that MAP remains a point-estimation method, whereas full Bayesian curve fitting requires integrating over all coefficient values.

nodes.title: 1.2.6 Bayesian curve fitting
nodes.summary: The text moves from maximum-likelihood polynomial regression to MAP and fully Bayesian curve fitting. It introduces a Gaussian prior over coefficients, shows that MAP estimation is equivalent to regularized least squares, and derives the Bayesian predictive distribution by integrating over the Gaussian posterior of the parameters. The resulting predictive mean and variance depend on the input, with variance reflecting both target noise and parameter uncertainty; an example is illustrated for a ninth-order polynomial. The text then introduces model selection, explaining model complexity, overfitting, training/validation/test splits, and cross-validation as a way to make efficient use of limited data.

This section develops probability theory from basic random variables, events, joint, marginal, conditional, sum, product, and Bayes rules using a fruit-box example, then extends these ideas to discrete, continuous, multivariate, and transformed distributions. It defines expectations, sample and conditional averages, variance, precision, and covariance, and presents Bayesian probability as rational uncertainty updating, contrasting it with frequentist methods and reviewing prior choice, inference, computation, and historical context. Gaussian distributions are developed in detail, including their moments, multivariate form, likelihoods, maximum-likelihood estimation, variance bias, and overfitting. These ideas are applied to polynomial curve fitting through maximum likelihood, MAP regularization, and fully Bayesian predictive distributions that account for parameter uncertainty, followed by model selection, data splitting, and cross-validation.

nodes.title: 1.3. Model Selection
nodes.summary: The text introduces model selection after Bayesian polynomial curve fitting. It explains how polynomial order, regularization, and other hyperparameters determine model complexity, why training performance is unreliable due to overfitting, and how validation and test sets can be used when data is plentiful. For limited data, it presents S-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation, including their benefits and computational drawbacks, especially with multiple hyperparameters. It then discusses training-data-based information criteria, particularly AIC and the forthcoming BIC, noting their complexity penalties and tendency to favor overly simple models because they ignore parameter uncertainty. A fully Bayesian treatment is proposed as a more principled alternative, followed by an introduction to the curse of dimensionality.

nodes.title: 1.4. The Curse of Dimensionality
nodes.summary: The text concludes a discussion of model evaluation and complexity selection, explaining S-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation, their computational and hyperparameter-search limitations, and information criteria such as AIC and BIC, while motivating Bayesian complexity penalties. It then introduces the curse of dimensionality through oil-flow classification, grid-cell methods, polynomial parameter growth, and geometric examples showing concentration of volume and Gaussian probability near high-dimensional surfaces. Although high dimensions create severe data and intuition problems, lower-dimensional manifolds and local smoothness make effective methods possible, as illustrated by image-based orientation recognition. Finally, it introduces decision theory, which uses inferred probabilities to make optimal predictions or actions in regression, classification, and medical diagnosis.

nodes.title: 1.5. Decision Theory
1.5.1 Minimizing the misclassification rate
nodes.summary: The text introduces decision theory for probabilistic classification, using Bayes’ theorem to relate priors, likelihoods, joint probabilities, and posterior class probabilities. It defines decision regions and boundaries, proves that minimum misclassification is achieved by assigning each input to the class with the highest posterior probability, and generalizes this result to multiple classes, with a graphical illustration for two classes. It then explains expected-loss minimization for situations where errors have unequal consequences, defines loss matrices and conditional expected loss, gives an asymmetric cancer-diagnosis example, and states that the optimal decision minimizes posterior-weighted loss for each input.

nodes.title: 1.5.2 Minimizing the expected loss
nodes.summary: The text presents decision theory for classification, emphasizing loss-sensitive decisions rather than merely minimizing error counts. It defines loss matrices, derives the rule of assigning each input to the class with minimum posterior expected loss, and illustrates the approach with asymmetric cancer-diagnosis costs. It then introduces a reject option for uncertain cases, controlled by a posterior threshold and extendable to loss-based rejection, before beginning the distinction between inference, which estimates posterior class probabilities, and decision-making, which acts on them.

nodes.title: 1.5.3 The reject option
nodes.summary: The text explains minimum-expected-loss classification using posterior probabilities, then introduces the reject option for uncertain inputs. Inputs whose highest posterior probability does not exceed threshold θ are rejected, allowing difficult cases to be handled separately; θ controls the rejection rate, with θ = 1 rejecting all cases and θ < 1/K rejecting none for K classes. The approach can incorporate rejection costs through a loss matrix. The section concludes by distinguishing inference, which learns p(C_k|x), from the subsequent decision stage.

nodes.title: 1.5.4 Inference and decision
nodes.summary: The text explains posterior-probability-based classification decisions, the uncertainty-based reject option, and three inference strategies: generative modeling, direct posterior (discriminative) modeling, and direct discriminant functions. It compares their costs and benefits, emphasizing that posterior probabilities support risk revision, rejection, class-prior correction, and probabilistic combination of models through the naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption. It then introduces regression loss functions, showing that squared loss is minimized by predicting the conditional mean of the target given the input.

nodes.title: 1.5.5 Loss functions for regression
nodes.summary: The text completes the naive Bayes discussion by applying conditional independence to combine X-ray and blood evidence, deriving the resulting class posterior, and explaining priors, normalization, and limitations of the factorization. It then develops regression decision theory: expected and squared loss, the conditional-mean regression function as the least-squares optimum, its error/irreducible-noise decomposition, three modeling approaches, and Minkowski losses whose optima range from mean to median to mode. Finally, it introduces information theory, defining information as probability-dependent surprise and motivating its logarithmic form through additivity for independent events.

This section introduces decision theory as the process of converting probabilistic inference into optimal predictions or actions. It develops Bayesian classification, first minimizing misclassification with maximum-posterior decisions and then minimizing posterior expected loss when errors have unequal costs. It covers decision regions, multiclass classification, asymmetric medical diagnosis, rejection of uncertain cases, and the distinction between inference and decision. It compares generative, posterior-based discriminative, and discriminant-function approaches, including naive Bayes combination of independent evidence and the roles of priors and normalization. The section then treats regression through expected, squared, and Minkowski losses, deriving the conditional mean, median, and mode as optimal predictors, discussing noise and modeling strategies, and concludes by introducing information theory through logarithmic measures of probabilistic surprise.

nodes.title: 1.6. Information Theory
Ludwig Boltzmann
nodes.summary: The text develops differential entropy as the continuous analogue of discrete entropy, explaining its divergent bin-width offset and its multidimensional definition. It maximizes differential entropy under normalization, fixed mean, and fixed variance using Lagrange multipliers, deriving the Gaussian as the maximum-entropy distribution and giving its entropy, including the possibility of negative differential entropy. It defines conditional entropy and establishes the entropy chain rule. It then introduces relative entropy or KL divergence as the extra coding cost of using an approximate distribution, notes its asymmetry and nonnegativity property, and begins proving that property through convexity. Biographical sidebars describe Boltzmann’s statistical interpretation of thermodynamic entropy and Shannon’s foundations of information theory, while appendices and exercises are referenced.

nodes.summary: The text explains mutual information as the Bayesian reduction in uncertainty produced by observing new data. It then presents five exercises covering least-squares polynomial fitting and its normal equations, regularized least squares, probability calculations involving mixtures of colored boxes and fruits, the transformation-dependent location of probability-density maxima under nonlinear and linear changes of variables, and a variance identity for a function f(x).

1.13 Suppose that the variance of a Gaussian is estimated using the result (1.56) but with the maximum likelihood estimate μML replaced with the true value μ of the mean. Show that this estimator has the property that its expectation is given by the true variance σ2.
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 1.12–1.23 from an introductory chapter. They cover Gaussian second moments and unbiased variance estimation; symmetric and antisymmetric matrix decompositions and polynomial parameter counts; recursive and closed-form counts of coefficients in multivariate polynomials and their asymptotic growth; Gamma-function identities; surface areas and volumes of spheres in arbitrary dimensions; high-dimensional geometry and concentration near cube corners; radial concentration of high-dimensional Gaussian distributions; an upper bound on two-class classification error; the interpretation of zero-one loss; and the general Bayes decision rule for arbitrary loss matrices and priors.

nodes.title: 1.21 Consider two nonnegative numbers a and b, and show that, if a ≥ b, then a ≥ (ab)1/2. Use this result to show that, if the decision regions of a two-class classification problem are chosen to minimize the probability of misclassification, this probability will satisfy p(mistake) ≤ ∫{p(x, C1)p(x, C2)}1/2 dx.
nodes.summary: Exercises 1.20–1.23 cover the concentration of high-dimensional Gaussian probability in a thin shell away from the origin; a bound on the optimal two-class Bayes error using the geometric-mean overlap of class densities; the reduction of zero-one loss to maximum-posterior classification; and the general minimum-expected-loss decision rule for arbitrary loss matrices and class priors.

nodes.title: 1.23 Derive the criterion for minimizing the expected loss when there is a general loss matrix and general prior probabilities for the classes.
nodes.summary: Exercises 1.20–1.30 cover high-dimensional Gaussian radial concentration; a geometric-mean bound on two-class Bayes error; zero-one, general-cost, and reject-option classification decisions; conditional means, medians, and modes as optimal regression predictors under different losses; the logarithmic form and upper bound of entropy; and the closed-form KL divergence between two univariate Gaussian distributions.

nodes.title: 1.26 By expansion of the square in (1.151), derive a result analogous to (1.90) and hence show that the function y(x) that minimizes the expected squared loss for the case of a vector t of target variables is again given by the conditional expectation of t.
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Bayesian decision-making with classification losses and rejection, showing that zero-one loss leads to a posterior-probability rejection threshold θ = 1 − λ. It then treats vector-valued regression under squared and L_q losses, establishing conditional means, medians, and modes as the respective optimal predictors. Further exercises derive the logarithmic form of entropy from additivity, prove the entropy upper bound ln M for an M-state variable, and compute the closed-form KL divergence between two univariate Gaussian distributions.

nodes.title: 1.28 In Section 1.6, we introduced the idea of entropy h(x) as the information gained on observing the value of a random variable x having distribution p(x). We saw that, for independent variables x and y for which p(x, y) = p(x)p(y), the entropy functions are additive, so that h(x, y) = h(x) + h(y). In this exercise, we derive the relation between h and p in the form of a function h(p). First show that h(p2) = 2h(p), and hence by induction that h(pn) = nh(p) where n is a positive integer. Hence show that h(pn/m) = (n/m)h(p) where m is also a positive integer. This implies that h(px) = xh(p) where x is a positive rational number, and hence by continuity when it is a positive real number. Finally, show that this implies h(p) must take the form h(p) ∝ ln p.
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on decision theory, regression losses, and information theory: deriving optimal classification with rejection and its threshold relation; proving that conditional means minimize vector squared loss and examining its decomposition; characterizing Lq-loss minimizers as conditional medians or modes; deriving the logarithmic form of entropy from additivity; proving the maximum entropy bound ln M for an M-state variable using Jensen’s inequality; and calculating the KL divergence between two Gaussian distributions.

nodes.title: 1.30 Evaluate the Kullback-Leibler divergence (1.113) between two Gaussians p(x) = N(x|μ, σ2) and q(x) = N(x|m, s2).
nodes.summary: Exercises 1.24–1.39 cover minimum-risk classification with rejection, conditional-mean/median/mode estimators under regression losses, foundational entropy derivations and bounds, Gaussian KL divergence and maximum-entropy results, entropy transformations and independence properties, convexity and Jensen-inequality proofs, and calculations of marginal, conditional, joint entropy and mutual information for a specified binary distribution.

nodes.title: 1.33 Suppose that the conditional entropy H[y|x] between two discrete random variables x and y is zero. Show that, for all values of x such that p(x) > 0, the variable y must be a function of x, in other words for each x there is only one value of y such that p(y|x) ≠ 0.
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 1.31–1.39 on entropy, probability, convexity, and maximum-entropy distributions. It asks for proofs of subadditivity of joint entropy and its independence equality condition, entropy transformation under linear mappings, the deterministic implication of zero conditional entropy, and the Gaussian maximum-entropy result via calculus of variations. It also covers deriving Gaussian entropy, characterizing strict convexity through the second derivative, proving a convexity identity using the probability product rule, extending a convex-function inequality by induction, and computing and diagramming multiple entropy and mutual-information quantities for a specified binary joint distribution.

nodes.title: 1.36 A strictly convex function is defined as one for which every chord lies above the function. Show that this is equivalent to the condition that the second derivative of the function be positive.
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 1.31–1.39 on entropy, probability, convexity, and Gaussian distributions. It asks for proofs of the subadditivity and independence condition for joint entropy, the entropy transformation rule under nonsingular linear mappings, the deterministic implication of zero conditional entropy, and the maximum-entropy Gaussian result using calculus of variations and constraints. It also covers deriving Gaussian entropy, characterizing strict convexity through the second derivative, proving a probability-based convexity result, extending the convexity inequality by induction, and computing and diagramming several entropy and mutual-information quantities for a binary joint distribution given in Table 1.3.

nodes.title: 1.37 Using the definition (1.111) together with the product rule of probability, prove the result (1.112).
nodes.summary: This section presents Exercises 1.31–1.41 on entropy, probability, convexity, and information theory. The problems cover subadditivity and independence of entropy, entropy changes under linear transformations, deterministic relationships implied by zero conditional entropy, the variational derivation and entropy of Gaussian maximum-entropy distributions, the characterization of strict convexity, proofs of convexity inequalities, calculations and graphical relationships among entropy and mutual information for a binary joint distribution, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality via Jensen’s inequality, and a probability-based identity for mutual information.

The section contains exercises spanning Gaussian estimation, matrix and polynomial coefficient counting, Gamma-function and hypersphere calculations, high-dimensional geometric and Gaussian concentration, Bayesian classification and decision theory, regression under several losses, and foundational information theory. It derives optimal predictors and decision rules, entropy's logarithmic form and bounds, Gaussian maximum-entropy and KL-divergence results, entropy transformation and independence properties, and a range of convexity and Jensen-inequality identities, including applications to binary entropy and mutual information.

The section surveys probability, statistics, decision theory, and information theory. It develops Gaussian and geometric results, estimation and regression methods, Bayesian classification, entropy and maximum-entropy principles, conditional and joint entropy, convexity and Jensen's inequality, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence. It connects KL divergence with coding efficiency, density estimation, and maximum likelihood, and concludes with mutual information as a nonnegative measure of dependence and uncertainty reduction, supported by exercises covering these topics.

The section introduces probability, statistics, decision theory, and information theory, developing Gaussian and geometric results, estimation and regression, Bayesian classification, and entropy-based concepts including conditional, joint, and maximum entropy. It presents convexity and Jensen's inequality, explains Kullback–Leibler divergence and its connections to coding efficiency, density estimation, and maximum likelihood, and concludes with mutual information as a nonnegative measure of dependence and uncertainty reduction, reinforced by exercises.

The section moves from Minkowski-based regression losses to foundational information theory. It defines information content and entropy, demonstrates their coding interpretation and relation to disorder, then develops differential, conditional, and maximum entropy, showing that the Gaussian is the maximum-entropy distribution under moment constraints. It introduces convexity, Jensen's inequality, relative entropy/Kullback–Leibler divergence and its coding, estimation, and likelihood connections, and mutual information as a measure of dependence and uncertainty reduction. Historical biographical material on Boltzmann and Shannon, plus referenced exercises and appendices, complements the theoretical development.

This section introduces pattern recognition and machine learning through handwritten-digit recognition, explaining supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, preprocessing, feature extraction, training, testing, and generalization. It develops polynomial curve fitting to illustrate regression, underfitting, overfitting, regularization, likelihood, Bayesian inference, and model selection. Probability theory is built from basic rules through distributions, moments, Gaussian models, Bayesian updating, and predictive inference. The section then treats validation, cross-validation, information criteria, Bayesian complexity control, and the curse of dimensionality. It explains decision theory for classification and regression under different losses, including medical diagnosis and uncertainty rejection, and concludes with information theory covering entropy, coding, maximum entropy, divergence, mutual information, convexity, and related historical context.

nodes.title: 2 Probability Distributions
2.1. Binary Variables
2.1.1 The beta distribution
nodes.summary: This section derives the mean and variance of the binomial distribution, introduces the beta distribution as a conjugate Bayesian prior for the Bernoulli parameter, and gives its normalization, moments, illustrative shapes, and posterior update. Observations add to the beta hyperparameters, which represent effective prior counts, and updating can be performed sequentially for online or large-scale learning. The predictive probability is the posterior mean, combining prior and observed frequencies; it converges to the maximum-likelihood result with abundant data, while posterior uncertainty generally decreases. A general mean and variance decomposition explains this reduction on average, while noting that individual data sets can behave differently. The section concludes by introducing multinomial variables and the 1-of-K representation, with references to Exercises 2.4–2.8.

This section develops probability models for binary outcomes, beginning with the Bernoulli distribution and its moments, likelihood, sufficient statistic, and maximum-likelihood estimate. It extends the model to counts of successes through the binomial distribution, then introduces Bayesian estimation using the conjugate beta prior, deriving its moments, posterior updating, sequential-learning interpretation, predictive probabilities, and uncertainty behavior. The section concludes by introducing multinomial variables and the 1-of-K representation.

nodes.title: 2.2. Multinomial Variables
2.2.1 The Dirichlet distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the maximum-likelihood estimate and multinomial distribution for category counts, including its combinatorial normalization and count constraint. It introduces the Dirichlet distribution as the multinomial’s conjugate prior on a K−1-dimensional simplex, gives its normalized form and posterior update, and interprets its parameters as effective observations; it also relates the binary binomial/beta and two-category multinomial/Dirichlet representations. A biographical note discusses mathematician Johann Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet. The text then begins the Gaussian-distribution section, presenting the univariate and multivariate forms and explaining its roles in maximum entropy and the central limit theorem.

This section generalizes Bernoulli variables to K-category multinomial variables using one-hot representations, develops their probabilities, likelihood, sufficient statistics, and maximum-likelihood estimates, and derives the multinomial count distribution. It then presents the Dirichlet distribution as the multinomial’s conjugate prior, including normalization, posterior updating, effective-count interpretation, and its relationship to the beta/binomial case, followed by a note on Dirichlet’s biography and an opening introduction to Gaussian distributions and their significance.

nodes.title: 2.3. The Gaussian Distribution
nodes.summary: The text transitions from Dirichlet and binary/multinomial modeling to an introduction of the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, giving their parameterized formulas and explaining their roles as maximum-entropy distributions and as limits of sums through the central limit theorem. Uniform-variable means and the binomial distribution are presented as examples of convergence toward Gaussian forms. The section is noted to be mathematically technical, especially regarding matrix identities, and begins discussing Gaussian geometry. It concludes with a biographical sidebar on Carl Friedrich Gauss and his mathematical and scientific contributions.

This section introduces probability distributions as fundamental tools for density estimation, assuming independent and identically distributed data, and uses simple models to develop statistical ideas such as likelihood, sufficient statistics, maximum-likelihood estimation, and Bayesian inference. It covers Bernoulli, binomial, multinomial, beta, and Dirichlet distributions, including their moments, conjugate updating, predictive behavior, and count interpretations. It then introduces univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, explaining their formulas, maximum-entropy status, geometric properties, technical matrix treatment, and emergence through the central limit theorem, with illustrative convergence examples and biographical notes on Dirichlet and Gauss.

nodes.title: Appendix C
Carl Friedrich Gauss
nodes.summary: The text explains why averages of many random variables, including the binomial distribution, approach a Gaussian and introduces the Gaussian’s geometric and algebraic structure. Its quadratic form defines Mahalanobis distance, while covariance eigenvectors and eigenvalues produce shifted, rotated coordinates in which constant-density surfaces are ellipsoids and the distribution factorizes into independent univariate Gaussians. Positive definiteness, Jacobian and determinant properties establish normalization. The mean and covariance are derived as μ and Σ, respectively. The text then discusses the Gaussian’s parameter-count and computational limitations, restricted covariance models, inability to represent multimodality, and the use of latent variables and structured graphical models to overcome these issues. It introduces partitioned conditional Gaussian distributions and precision matrices, including their symmetry properties, and starts deriving the conditional density. A sidebar provides biographical information about Carl Friedrich Gauss and his contributions.

nodes.title: 2.3.1 Conditional Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional Gaussian distributions for partitioned jointly Gaussian variables, defines the corresponding covariance and precision-matrix partitions, and derives the conditional mean and covariance by expanding the Gaussian quadratic form and completing the square. It gives equivalent formulas in precision form and covariance form using a block-matrix inverse and the Schur complement, emphasizing that the conditional mean is linear in the observed variables and the conditional covariance is constant, thereby forming a linear-Gaussian model.

nodes.title: 2.3.2 Marginal Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal of a partitioned multivariate Gaussian by completing the square in x_b and integrating it out. It shows that the marginal remains Gaussian with mean μ_a and covariance (Λ_aa − Λ_abΛ_bb^{-1}Λ_ba)^{-1} = Σ_aa, and summarizes these results alongside the conditional Gaussian formulas. It explains that precision matrices are most useful for conditionals, covariance matrices for marginals, illustrates the distributions graphically, and begins introducing Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables with linear-mean, constant-covariance conditionals.

nodes.title: 2.3.3 Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables
nodes.summary: The text explains marginal and conditional distributions for partitioned multivariate Gaussians, illustrated by a two-variable example, and develops Bayes’ theorem for a linear Gaussian model. It derives the joint precision, covariance, and mean, then obtains the marginal distribution of y and posterior distribution of x given y, including the Gaussian convolution special case. It concludes by introducing maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian, identifying its sufficient statistics and deriving the sample-mean estimate of the mean.

nodes.title: 2.3.4 Maximum likelihood for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal and conditional distributions for jointly related Gaussian variables, then develops maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian. It identifies the first- and second-moment sums as sufficient statistics, derives the sample mean and covariance maximum-likelihood estimators, explains that the mean estimate is unbiased while the covariance estimate is biased by a factor (N−1)/N, and gives the unbiased covariance correction. It concludes by introducing sequential estimation, in which data are processed one observation at a time for online or large-scale applications.

nodes.title: 2.3.5 Sequential estimation
nodes.summary: The text completes the maximum-likelihood treatment of a multivariate Gaussian by deriving the covariance estimator, showing that the mean estimate is unbiased while the covariance estimate is biased downward, and giving the standard unbiased covariance correction. It then introduces sequential estimation, derives the recursive update for the Gaussian mean, and develops the Robbins–Monro method for finding roots of regression functions, including its convergence conditions and interpretation. Maximum-likelihood estimation is recast as a root-finding problem for the expected score, and the method is applied to Gaussian mean estimation, recovering the recursive mean update and extending to multivariate settings. Finally, the text begins Bayesian Gaussian inference by introducing priors and presenting the likelihood for estimating a mean with known variance.

nodes.title: 2.3.6 Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of Gaussian sequential estimation by showing that the log-likelihood regression function is linear, its root is the maximum-likelihood mean, and the sequential update uses a_N = σ²/N, with a multivariate extension. It then develops Bayesian Gaussian inference: a Gaussian prior for an unknown mean with known variance yields a Gaussian posterior whose mean combines prior and sample information through precisions and whose variance decreases with data; sequential Bayesian updating follows naturally. For unknown variance, inference is expressed in terms of precision and uses a gamma conjugate prior, producing gamma posterior parameters and an effective-prior-observation interpretation. With both mean and precision unknown, the conjugate prior is normal-gamma; multivariate analogues are Gaussian, Wishart, and normal-Wishart distributions, with inverse Wishart for covariance. Figures illustrate the Gaussian posterior, gamma distributions, and normal-gamma contours, and the section concludes by introducing Student’s t-distribution as the result of integrating out Gaussian precision.

nodes.title: 2.3.7 Student’s t-distribution
nodes.summary: The text introduces Wishart and normal-Wishart conjugate priors for multivariate Gaussian precision and mean parameters, briefly noting the inverse Wishart alternative. It derives the univariate Student’s t-distribution by integrating a Gaussian precision under a Gamma prior, explains its parameterization, limiting cases, Gaussian-mixture interpretation, heavy tails, robustness to outliers, and relevance to regression, with supporting figures. It then extends the construction to the multivariate t-distribution, giving its density, Mahalanobis-distance form, mean, covariance, and mode. Finally, it motivates special treatment of periodic variables because ordinary averages and Gaussian models depend on the angular origin, and introduces unit-circle vector representations for invariant averaging.

nodes.title: 2.3.8 Periodic variables
nodes.summary: The text first specifies the multivariate Student’s t-distribution and its moment and mode properties. It then explains why ordinary Gaussians are unsuitable for periodic variables, develops an origin-invariant circular mean using unit vectors, and derives the von Mises distribution by conditioning an isotropic two-dimensional Gaussian on the unit circle. The von Mises parameters, Bessel-function normalization, large-concentration approximation, and maximum-likelihood estimates are presented. Alternative periodic modeling methods and mixtures of von Mises distributions for multimodality are discussed. Finally, the text introduces mixtures of Gaussians as a way to model multimodal data, illustrated by the two-cluster Old Faithful dataset.

nodes.title: 2.3.9 Mixtures of Gaussians
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of periodic distributions and introduces Gaussian mixtures as a flexible way to represent multimodal data, illustrated by the two-cluster Old Faithful data set. It defines mixture densities, constraints and probabilistic interpretations of mixing coefficients, derives component responsibilities, and explains that maximum-likelihood estimation requires numerical optimization or expectation maximization. 2.5.1 Kernel density estimators

Kernel estimation fixes the region size, defines a hypercube Parzen window, and generalizes it to smooth kernels such as Gaussians, whose bandwidth h controls the trade-off between noise and oversmoothing. Valid kernels are nonnegative and normalized; the method has no training computation but has evaluation cost linear in dataset size. Nearest-neighbour estimation instead fixes the number of points and adapts neighbourhood volume to local density, addressing the shortcomings of a globally fixed bandwidth.

nodes.title: 2.5.2 Nearest-neighbour methods

K-nearest-neighbour density estimation instead fixes the number K of points and adapts the local volume, but does not produce a globally integrable density. Applying the method class by class and Bayes’ theorem yields p(C_k|x) = K_k/K, so classification is by the majority among the K nearest training points, with K = 1 giving the nearest-neighbour rule. nodes.title: 3 Linear Models for Regression
3.1. Linear Basis Function Models
3.1.1 Maximum likelihood and least squares
nodes.summary: The text introduces linear basis-function regression and relates least squares to maximum likelihood under additive Gaussian noise. It defines the Gaussian model, conditional-mean prediction, likelihood, log likelihood, sum-of-squares error, normal equations, design matrix, pseudoinverse, bias interpretation, and maximum-likelihood noise precision. It also explains the geometric projection interpretation of least squares, discusses numerical problems from collinear basis functions and remedies using SVD or regularization, and motivates sequential learning for large data sets. Basis-function choices and the scope of the discussion, including wavelets, identity features, and single versus multiple targets, are also noted.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Geometry of least squares
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometric interpretation of least squares: predictions formed from basis functions lie in a subspace, and the optimal regression prediction is the orthogonal projection of the target vector onto that subspace, with error equal to squared Euclidean distance and inverse noise precision related to residual variance. It also discusses numerical instability from nearly dependent basis functions, recommending SVD or regularization, and introduces sequential learning as a more scalable alternative to batch processing for large data sets.

It discusses instability from collinear basis vectors and remedies such as SVD and regularization. It then introduces sequential learning for large or streaming datasets, derives stochastic gradient descent and the LMS update rule, and emphasizes the importance of the learning rate. Finally, it presents regularized least squares, defines quadratic weight regularization, and explains its roles as weight decay and parameter shrinkage for controlling overfitting.

Numerical instability from collinear bases motivates SVD, regularization, and sequential stochastic-gradient or LMS learning for large or streaming datasets. Regularized least squares is developed through quadratic and l_q penalties, including lasso sparsity and complexity control. The treatment is extended to multiple outputs with shared bases and matrix weights, and concludes with the bias-variance view of model complexity, overfitting, regularization selection, and the contrast between frequentist fitting and Bayesian parameter marginalization.

nodes.title: 3.2. The Bias-Variance Decomposition
nodes.summary: The text first derives the maximum-likelihood solution for multivariate linear regression, showing that target variables decouple and share a design-matrix pseudo-inverse. It then develops the frequentist bias-variance decomposition: expected squared prediction loss consists of squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise, with flexible models trading lower bias for higher variance. A sinusoidal-data experiment demonstrates how regularization controls this trade-off, identifies an approximately optimal regularization value, and shows the value of averaging predictions. Because the decomposition relies on unavailable ensembles of data sets, the text turns to Bayesian linear regression as a practical approach to avoiding overfitting and selecting model complexity, beginning with a Gaussian prior over the weights under known noise precision.

nodes.title: 3.3. Bayesian Linear Regression
3.3.1 Parameter distribution
nodes.summary: The text moves from the limitations of frequentist bias-variance analysis and hold-out model selection to Bayesian linear regression as a principled way to control overfitting and infer model complexity from training data. It develops Gaussian priors and posteriors for linear-model weights, gives their parameter formulas and sequential-update interpretation, relates the MAP solution to quadratic regularization, and illustrates learning with a noisy straight-line example. It also discusses non-Gaussian priors and their connection to other regularizers, then derives the Gaussian predictive distribution, showing how its variance combines noise and parameter uncertainty and decreases with additional data.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text generalizes the weight prior beyond the Gaussian case and explains its relationship to regularized error minimization and posterior modes. It derives the Gaussian predictive distribution for Bayesian linear regression, separating predictive uncertainty into observation noise and parameter uncertainty, and discusses how uncertainty changes with data quantity and input location. Examples using noisy sinusoidal data illustrate predictive means, variances, and posterior function samples. The text also addresses overconfident extrapolation with localized basis functions, notes the Student's t predictive distribution obtained when noise precision is unknown, and introduces the equivalent-kernel interpretation of the posterior mean as a localized linear smoother over training targets.

nodes.title: 3.3.3 Equivalent kernel
nodes.summary: The text explains the equivalent kernel in Bayesian linear regression: the predictive mean is a linear combination of training targets whose input-dependent weights are localized, sum to one under stated conditions, may be negative, and can be written as an inner product. The kernel also determines covariance and joint predictive uncertainty, motivating Gaussian processes. It then introduces Bayesian model comparison, in which models are assigned prior probabilities and compared using posterior probabilities and model evidence, avoiding overfitting, validation sets, and repeated cross-validation while allowing multiple complexity parameters to be learned from the training data.

This section develops Bayesian linear regression as a framework for regularization, uncertainty quantification, and model-complexity selection. It derives Gaussian weight priors, posteriors, MAP regularization, predictive distributions, and their noise and parameter-uncertainty components, while discussing non-Gaussian priors, Student's t predictions, sequential learning, and illustrative line and sinusoid examples. It interprets predictions through an equivalent kernel that provides localized weights and covariance structure, motivating Gaussian processes, and concludes with Bayesian model comparison based on posterior probabilities and model evidence.

nodes.title: 3.4. Bayesian Model Comparison
nodes.summary: The text first notes the signed, inner-product form of the equivalent kernel. It then develops Bayesian model comparison as an alternative to cross-validation: posterior model probabilities combine model priors with the parameter-marginalized evidence, Bayes factors compare evidences, and predictions can average all models or select the most probable one. Evidence is the normalization integral over parameters and balances data fit against an Occam-style complexity penalty, explaining why intermediate-complexity models may be preferred and why, on average, the correct model wins when it is included. The method remains dependent on appropriate, proper priors and model assumptions, so independent testing is advisable. Finally, the evidence approximation for linear regression is introduced, fixing hyperparameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood and approximating full hyperparameter marginalization when their posterior is sharply concentrated.

nodes.title: 3.5. The Evidence Approximation
3.5.1 Evaluation of the evidence function
nodes.summary: This section introduces the evidence approximation for Bayesian linear regression: α and β, which control prior and noise precision, can be learned from training data by maximizing the marginal likelihood rather than using cross-validation. It discusses alternative Gamma-prior and Laplace-approximation approaches, explaining why skewness can make Laplace inferior, and notes the equivalence of analytical evidence maximization and EM. The evidence is evaluated by integrating over weights, completing the square in the regularized error, identifying the Hessian A and posterior mean m_N, and applying Gaussian normalization to obtain the log-evidence formula. A polynomial-regression example shows how evidence trades data fit against complexity and selects a cubic model. Finally, eigenvalue analysis of A is used to derive the stationary condition for optimizing α.

nodes.title: 3.5.2 Maximizing the evidence function
nodes.summary: The text explains why Bayesian model evidence selects a cubic polynomial despite similar generalization errors among several higher-order models, balancing fit improvement against complexity. It then derives iterative evidence-maximization updates for the prior precision alpha and noise precision beta using the eigenvalues of beta Phi^T Phi, the posterior mode, and the effective parameter count gamma. Gamma quantifies how many parameter directions are constrained by the data, distinguishing likelihood-dominated from prior-dominated directions, and modifies the variance estimate by replacing the usual N denominator with N - gamma.

nodes.title: 3.5.3 Effective number of parameters
nodes.summary: The text explains the eigenvalue-based shrinkage of MAP regression parameters, defines the effective parameter count γ as the number of directions constrained by the data, and shows how it yields the N−γ correction in Bayesian variance estimation. It relates this correction to the familiar N−1 unbiased Gaussian variance estimate, presents an evidence-based example for selecting α in a ten-parameter Gaussian-basis sinusoidal model, and describes how α, γ, the evidence maximum, and generalization error are connected. In the large-data limit, γ=M and the hyperparameter updates simplify. The section concludes by introducing the limitations of fixed nonlinear basis functions while emphasizing their analytical and Bayesian tractability.

This section presents the evidence approximation for Bayesian linear regression, using empirical Bayes to optimize the prior and noise precisions after integrating out the weights. It derives and evaluates the marginal likelihood, discusses alternative approximations, and shows how evidence selects models by balancing fit and complexity. Eigenvalue analysis yields iterative hyperparameter updates and the effective parameter count γ, which explains parameter shrinkage and the N−γ variance correction. Examples demonstrate model and hyperparameter selection and their connection to generalization, while the section also highlights evidence sensitivity to priors, the problems with improper priors, the value of independent test data, and the limitations and tractability of fixed basis-function models.

nodes.title: 3.6. Limitations of Fixed Basis Functions
nodes.summary: The text interprets evidence optimization through plots showing that the intersection of γ and 2αE_W identifies the optimal regularization parameter, coincides with the log-evidence maximum, and gives near-best test performance; it also illustrates how model weights vary with effective parameter count. It then summarizes the strengths of fixed-basis linear regression and their main limitation: the curse of dimensionality caused by choosing basis functions before seeing the data. Lower-dimensional data manifolds, localized bases, and neural networks with adaptive bases help address this limitation, while later chapters introduce more complex models. The exercise proves the relationship between logistic sigmoid and tanh functions and derives the corresponding reparameterization of their linear combinations.

nodes.title: 4 Linear Models for Classification
4.1. Discriminant Functions
4.1.1 Two classes
nodes.summary: The text introduces linear discriminant functions for classification, contrasting their nonlinear-parameter extensions with regression and noting that basis-function transformations can also be used. It defines binary linear discriminants, explains how the weight vector controls the hyperplane’s orientation, how the bias controls its location, and how the discriminant value gives signed distance from the boundary. It also presents augmented-vector notation and begins the discussion of multiclass classification, warning that a one-versus-the-rest combination of binary classifiers leads to difficulties.

nodes.title: 4.1.2 Multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometry and signed distance of binary linear decision surfaces, introduces augmented-vector notation, and extends linear discriminants to multiple classes. It describes why one-versus-the-rest and one-versus-one binary schemes can create ambiguous regions, then presents a unified K-function discriminant whose pairwise boundaries are hyperplanes and whose decision regions are convex and singly connected. It notes the equivalence of the binary formulations and introduces least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as parameter-learning approaches. The least-squares section begins by relating 1-of-K targets to conditional class probabilities, while warning that linear approximations may be inaccurate or fall outside the probability range, and gives the vector form of the class models.

nodes.title: 4.1.3 Least squares for classification
nodes.summary: The text proves that multiclass linear discriminant regions are convex and singly connected, notes equivalent formulations for binary classification, and introduces least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as parameter-learning methods. It develops the least-squares formulation for K-class 1-of-K targets, including its matrix representation, pseudoinverse solution, and prediction-sum constraint, while explaining why outputs are not probabilities. It then details least squares’ sensitivity to outliers, excessive correctness penalties, and poor multiclass behavior, illustrated by two figures, and attributes these weaknesses to its inappropriate Gaussian assumption before introducing Fisher’s linear discriminant.

nodes.title: 4.1.4 Fisher’s linear discriminant
nodes.summary: The text critiques least-squares classification for its outlier sensitivity and poor performance on multiclass data, explaining that its Gaussian likelihood assumption is unsuitable for binary targets and motivating better probabilistic models such as logistic regression. It then introduces Fisher’s linear discriminant as a projection-based classifier: data are projected onto one dimension, and the projection is chosen to maximize between-class separation relative to within-class variance. Derivation of the Fisher criterion leads to the direction w proportional to S_W^{-1}(m_2 − m_1), reducing to the mean-difference direction for isotropic covariance. The projected data can then be classified using a threshold, potentially derived from Gaussian class models. Finally, the text starts comparing Fisher’s method with least squares and notes that Fisher’s criterion is a special case of least squares under alternative target coding for two classes.

nodes.title: 4.1.5 Relation to least squares
nodes.summary: The passage derives Fisher’s linear discriminant by maximizing the ratio of between-class to within-class projected variance, obtaining the projection direction w ∝ S_W^{-1}(m_2 − m_1), with the isotropic-covariance case reducing to the difference of class means. It explains how a threshold, optionally based on Gaussian models of the projected classes, converts this projection into a classifier. It then shows that, for two classes and a particular target coding, the least-squares classifier produces the same weight direction as Fisher’s criterion, while also yielding the bias w0 = −w^T m and the classification rule y(x) = w^T(x − m) > 0 for class C1.

nodes.title: 4.1.6 Fisher’s discriminant for multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text develops Fisher’s discriminant for multiple classes by defining within-class, total, and between-class covariance matrices in the original and projected spaces. It formulates a trace-based objective that favors large between-class and small within-class covariance, solves it using the leading generalized eigenvectors, and shows that at most K - 1 discriminant features can be obtained because the between-class covariance has rank at most K - 1. It then introduces the perceptron as a two-class linear discriminant that applies a fixed nonlinear feature transformation before a generalized linear decision function.

nodes.title: 4.1.7 The perceptron algorithm
nodes.summary: The text first develops linear dimensionality reduction for classification by defining projected within- and between-class covariances, optimizing a trace criterion through generalized eigenvectors, and showing that at most K−1 discriminative features can be obtained. It then introduces the two-class perceptron, including its feature mapping, step activation, ±1 targets, perceptron error criterion, stochastic update rule, interpretation, convergence theorem, dependence on data separability and ordering, historical development, illustrative figures, hardware implementations, and limitations. The related adaline is mentioned, followed by a transition from discriminative models to probabilistic generative classification.

This section develops linear discriminant functions for binary and multiclass classification, covering their geometry, augmented notation, basis-function extensions, and the problems of combining binary classifiers. It presents least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as learning methods: least squares is formulated for 1-of-K targets but critiqued for nonprobabilistic outputs, outlier sensitivity, poor multiclass behavior, and inappropriate assumptions; Fisher’s method projects data to maximize between-class relative to within-class variance, relates to least squares, and generalizes through covariance matrices and generalized eigenvectors to at most K−1 features; and the perceptron is described through its feature mapping, activation, error function, update rule, convergence, practical history, and limitations. The section ends by pointing toward probabilistic generative classifiers.

nodes.title: 4.2. Probabilistic Generative Models
4.2.1 Continuous inputs
nodes.summary: The text develops probabilistic generative classification using logistic and softmax posteriors. It shows that Gaussian class-conditional distributions with a shared covariance produce linear discriminants and linear decision boundaries, while class-specific covariances produce quadratic boundaries; class priors shift boundaries through bias terms. It then introduces maximum-likelihood estimation for a two-class Gaussian model, specifying the labeled-data likelihood in terms of the class prior, means, and shared covariance, and notes that log-likelihood maximization is used to estimate these parameters.

nodes.title: 4.2.2 Maximum likelihood solution
nodes.summary: The text illustrates how Gaussian class covariances determine linear or quadratic decision boundaries, then derives maximum likelihood estimates for a two-class Gaussian generative classifier: class priors equal class frequencies, class means equal within-class sample means, and the shared covariance is the pooled within-class covariance. It notes the lack of robustness to outliers. It then introduces discrete features, explaining the exponential parameter growth of unrestricted distributions and the naive Bayes conditional-independence simplification, which gives linear log-probability functions and logistic-sigmoid formulations for binary classification, with analogous extensions to multicategory features. Finally, it begins the discussion of exponential-family models and generalized linear posterior probabilities.

nodes.title: 4.2.3 Discrete features
nodes.summary: The text derives the maximum-likelihood shared covariance for Gaussian class-conditional models as a sample-size-weighted combination of the within-class covariance matrices, notes its extension to K classes, and cautions that Gaussian fitting is sensitive to outliers. It then treats discrete features, explaining why unrestricted binary-feature distributions are exponentially large and how the naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption reduces the parameters to D per class. The resulting log discriminants are linear in the inputs, with binary two-class models expressible through logistic sigmoid functions and analogous formulations for multistate discrete variables. It begins a broader discussion of the exponential family and generalized linear posterior class models.

nodes.title: 4.2.4 Exponential family
nodes.summary: The text completes the shared-covariance Gaussian classifier by defining the pooled covariance as a weighted combination of within-class covariances, noting its extension to K classes and its lack of robustness to outliers. It then develops naive Bayes models for binary and general discrete features, showing that conditional independence leads to linear log-posterior functions. The same linear-logit or linear-softmax structure is derived for a restricted exponential-family class of distributions with shared scale. Finally, it introduces probabilistic discriminative models, contrasting direct maximum-likelihood estimation of generalized linear model parameters—solvable by IRLS—with the indirect generative approach of fitting class distributions and priors before applying Bayes' theorem.

This section develops probabilistic generative classification from Bayes' theorem, deriving logistic-sigmoid and multiclass softmax posteriors from class likelihoods and priors. It analyzes Gaussian models, showing how shared or class-specific covariances produce linear or quadratic decision boundaries, derives their maximum-likelihood parameter estimates, and notes their sensitivity to outliers. It then treats discrete features through naive Bayes, explains the resulting linear logit structure, extends the analysis to exponential-family models, and contrasts indirect generative estimation with direct discriminative estimation using generalized linear models and IRLS.

nodes.title: 4.3. Probabilistic Discriminative Models
4.3.1 Fixed basis functions
nodes.summary: The text contrasts generative and discriminative classification, then introduces fixed nonlinear basis functions, which create feature spaces where linear decision boundaries represent nonlinear boundaries in the original input space. It discusses bias terms, overlapping class distributions, the inability of transformations to remove overlap, and the limitations and usefulness of fixed bases. It then presents two-class logistic regression as a sigmoid model of posterior class probability, compares its linearly growing parameter count with the quadratic cost of Gaussian generative models, and notes that maximum-likelihood training relies on the sigmoid derivative.

nodes.title: 4.3.2 Logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text introduces fixed nonlinear basis-function models for classification, noting the role of a bias basis function, the persistence of class overlap under transformations, and the limitations of nonadaptive features. It then develops two-class logistic regression, in which the posterior is a sigmoid of a linear feature function, compares its linear parameter growth with the quadratic growth of a Gaussian generative model, and derives its Bernoulli likelihood, cross-entropy error, and simplified gradient. The gradient supports sequential learning and resembles that of linear regression. Finally, it explains the infinite-weight overfitting problem for linearly separable data, the nonuniqueness of separating solutions, and the use of priors or regularization to resolve it.

nodes.title: 4.3.3 Iterative reweighted least squares
nodes.summary: The text develops Newton–Raphson optimization for logistic regression, first contrasting it with the one-step least-squares solution for quadratic linear-regression error. It derives the logistic cross-entropy gradient and Hessian, establishes uniqueness through the positive-definite Hessian, and reformulates the update as iterative reweighted least squares with variance-based weights and locally linearized effective targets. It then introduces multiclass logistic regression through softmax probabilities, derives the softmax Jacobian, formulates the 1-of-K likelihood and cross-entropy error, and gives the gradient with respect to each class’s parameter vector.

nodes.title: 4.3.4 Multiclass logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text develops multiclass logistic regression by expressing class probabilities through a softmax of linear activations, deriving the likelihood, multiclass cross-entropy error, softmax derivatives, and the simple error-times-feature gradient. It discusses sequential updates, Newton-Raphson and IRLS batch optimization, the block Hessian, its positive definiteness and unique minimum, and related exercises and references. It then introduces probit regression as an alternative binary discriminative model motivated by class-conditional distributions that do not yield logistic posteriors, defining a generalized linear activation and a threshold-based interpretation.

nodes.title: 4.3.5 Probit regression
nodes.summary: The text completes the multiclass logistic-regression optimization discussion by deriving its error-times-feature gradients, Newton–Raphson/IRLS Hessian structure, and unique minimum. It then introduces probit regression through a stochastic threshold model, deriving the activation function as a threshold CDF, specializing it to the Gaussian probit function and its relation to erf, and noting maximum-likelihood fitting, similarity to logistic regression, and Bayesian applications. It compares logistic and probit robustness to outliers, presents a probabilistic model for mislabeled targets, and begins the general theory of canonical link functions for exponential-family target distributions, including the resulting conditional-mean expression.

nodes.title: 4.3.6 Canonical link functions
nodes.summary: The text discusses classifier outliers, noting that input errors and mislabeled targets can distort decision boundaries and that probit regression is more sensitive to outliers than logistic regression because of its faster-decaying tails. Label noise is incorporated by modeling a target-flip probability ε, which may be fixed or learned. It then introduces canonical link functions for generalized linear models: exponential-family target distributions yield a mean–natural-parameter relationship, and choosing the activation as the inverse of the corresponding link causes likelihood gradients for Gaussian, logistic, and softmax models to simplify to a scaled prediction error times the feature vector. The section concludes by introducing the Laplace approximation and the greater difficulty of Bayesian logistic regression.

This section develops probabilistic discriminative classification from the observation that broad exponential-family class-conditional models yield linear logistic or softmax posterior activations. It introduces fixed basis functions and then derives binary and multiclass logistic regression, including their likelihoods, cross-entropy objectives, gradients, Hessians, Newton–Raphson optimization, and IRLS algorithms, while addressing separability, regularization, parameter scaling, and uniqueness. It also presents probit regression as a threshold-based alternative, compares logistic and probit robustness to outliers, models label noise, and explains canonical link functions for exponential-family generalized linear models. The section closes by introducing the Laplace approximation and the difficulties of Bayesian logistic regression.

nodes.title: 4.4. The Laplace Approximation
4.4.1 Model comparison and BIC
nodes.summary: The text explains the applicability, assumptions, and limitations of the Laplace approximation, emphasizing its usefulness for large-data posteriors but its inability to represent non-real variables directly or capture global and multimodal structure. It derives how the approximation estimates normalization constants and Bayesian model evidence, including the Hessian-based Occam factor, and shows how simplifying assumptions lead to the BIC complexity penalty, contrasting it with AIC and noting potential failures when parameters are poorly determined. It then introduces Bayesian logistic regression, for which exact posterior and predictive inference are intractable, and motivates using a Laplace approximation with a Gaussian weight prior.

The section introduces generalized linear models and the simplifying role of canonical link functions, then develops the Laplace approximation by replacing a density near a local mode with a Gaussian determined by its curvature. It gives the univariate and multivariate formulations, normalization, Hessian and positive-definiteness requirements, and numerical mode-finding procedure. It then describes applications to normalization constants and Bayesian model evidence, including the Occam factor and BIC penalty, contrasts BIC with AIC and discusses limitations such as poorly determined or multimodal parameters, and motivates the approximation for Bayesian logistic regression with a Gaussian prior.

nodes.title: 4.5. Bayesian Logistic Regression

It then introduces a Gaussian-prior Bayesian logistic model, derives the MAP-centered Gaussian posterior and its Hessian-based covariance, and marginalizes this approximation to obtain predictive probabilities. The weight integral is reduced to a one-dimensional Gaussian integral over a = wTφ; because the sigmoid-Gaussian convolution is intractable, a slope-matched probit approximation gives a closed-form scaled-sigmoid prediction. Posterior uncertainty changes predictive probabilities but not the 0.5 decision boundary under equal misclassification costs. The excerpt ends with exercises on convex-hull characterization of linear separability and preservation of target linear constraints by least-squares predictions.
