It derives the associated likelihoods, posterior probabilities, optimization procedures, curvature properties, regularization and noise considerations, and linear or quadratic decision boundaries. The section also introduces the Laplace approximation, model evidence, Occam penalties, BIC and AIC, and Bayesian logistic regression with approximate posterior and predictive integration. Exercises reinforce the geometric, algebraic, statistical, optimization, Gaussian, sigmoid, probit, softmax, separability, constraint-preservation, and Bayesian-approximation results.

nodes.title: 5 Neural Networks
5.1. Feed-forward Network Functions
5.1.1 Weight-space symmetries
nodes.summary: The text illustrates feed-forward networks’ ability to approximate diverse functions and solve classification tasks, emphasizing collaborative hidden-unit behavior and maximum-likelihood and Bayesian training approaches. It then explains weight-space symmetries: sign flips of tanh hidden units and permutations of hidden units produce equivalent mappings, yielding an M!2^M symmetry factor for two-layer networks and multiplicative factors across deeper layers. These symmetries generally have limited practical impact but can affect Bayesian model comparison. Network training is introduced as fitting a nonlinear input-output mapping by minimizing a sum-of-squares error on paired training data.

This section develops feed-forward neural networks as layered, trainable nonlinear extensions of linear models. It defines weighted input-to-hidden and hidden-to-output transformations, biases, activation choices for regression and classification, and forward propagation, while explaining their deterministic network-diagram representation and equivalence to multilayer perceptrons. It discusses bias absorption, differentiability, the limitations of linear hidden layers, deeper and skip-connected architectures, and layer-count terminology. It also introduces the networks’ function-approximation and training roles, including error-based, maximum-likelihood, and Bayesian approaches, and explains hidden-unit permutation and sign-flip symmetries and their implications.

nodes.title: 5.2. Network Training
5.2.1 Parameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text explains the softmax output and its matching multiclass cross-entropy loss, including probability constraints, activation-shift degeneracy, and regularization, and summarizes the appropriate output/error combinations for regression and binary or multiclass classification. It then introduces neural-network parameter optimization through a geometric view of the error surface, explaining gradients, stationary points, local and global minima, equivalent solutions, and the difficulty of nonlinear optimization. Training therefore uses iterative numerical weight updates, often based on gradients, while a Taylor-series local quadratic approximation provides insight into optimization techniques.

nodes.title: 5.2.2 Local quadratic approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains neural-network training as numerical optimization of a nonlinear error function. Stationary points occur where the gradient vanishes and include minima, maxima, and saddle points; the landscape contains many equivalent minima caused by network symmetries, as well as multiple inequivalent local minima. The global minimum is usually impossible to identify analytically, so iterative update algorithms are used, often exploiting gradients. A Taylor expansion gives a local quadratic model defined by the gradient and Hessian. Around a minimum, the error is determined by the Hessian’s eigenvalues and eigenvectors: its contours are aligned ellipses, and the minimum requires a positive-definite Hessian (positive second derivative in one dimension). Efficient gradient evaluation through backpropagation can speed optimization, while the quadratic model otherwise involves O(W²) independent information for W parameters.

nodes.title: 5.2.3 Use of gradient information
nodes.summary: The text explains the quadratic geometry of error functions near stationary points, showing that Hessian eigenvectors define elliptical constant-error contours and that positive Hessian eigenvalues characterize minima. It then motivates gradient-based training by comparing its O(W^2) computational cost with the O(W^3) cost of gradient-free optimization. Basic batch gradient descent, its learning-rate update, limitations, and more efficient alternatives are described, along with the need for multiple random starts and validation. Finally, stochastic or online gradient descent is introduced as a per-data-point alternative for errors that decompose over independent observations.

nodes.title: 5.2.4 Gradient descent optimization
nodes.summary: The text explains why gradient information and error backpropagation make neural-network training computationally practical, reducing optimization from roughly O(W^3) to O(W^2). It introduces batch gradient descent, its learning-rate update rule and limitations, more effective conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton alternatives, repeated initialization with validation, and online or stochastic gradient descent, including its update rule, minibatch variants, efficiency with redundant data, and ability to escape some local minima. It then introduces error backpropagation as an efficient forward-and-backward method for computing weight derivatives, emphasizing that derivative evaluation is distinct from the optimization step and that backpropagation applies to broader network and error-function settings.

The section develops neural-network training from error minimization to probabilistic maximum-likelihood learning. It derives sum-of-squares regression from Gaussian outputs, Bernoulli cross-entropy for logistic binary classification, and softmax cross-entropy for multiclass classification, including output constraints and regularization considerations. It then treats training as difficult nonconvex optimization shaped by stationary points, local minima, saddle points, and network symmetries. Local Taylor and Hessian analyses explain curvature and elliptical error contours, motivating gradient-based methods. Batch, stochastic, and minibatch gradient descent, conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton alternatives, initialization and validation strategies, and the computational role of backpropagation are covered.

nodes.title: 5.3. Error Backpropagation
5.3.1 Evaluation of error-function derivatives
Error Backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text derives error backpropagation for hidden units using the chain rule, showing that each hidden-unit error signal is the activation derivative multiplied by a weighted sum of downstream error signals. It explains the direction and indexing of backward propagation, presents the complete four-step algorithm for computing derivatives, and describes summing pattern-wise derivatives for batch training and extending the method to unit-specific activations. It then introduces a two-layer illustrative network with tanh hidden units, linear outputs, and sum-of-squares error, giving the tanh function, its derivative, the error definition, and the forward-propagation equations.

The section develops error-function derivatives for general feed-forward neural networks. It begins with per-pattern error decomposition and a linear sum-of-squares example, then generalizes via forward propagation, chain-rule error signals, and the local gradient formula δjzi, including output and hidden-unit backpropagation. It gives the full derivative-computation algorithm, batch-training accumulation, and support for unit-specific activations, and concludes with a two-layer tanh-hidden, linear-output example while relating derivative computation to broader optimization and higher-order derivatives.

nodes.title: 5.3.2 A simple example
nodes.summary: The text completes the batch backpropagation result, noting that total-error gradients are sums over patterns and that units may use different activation functions. It then presents a two-layer tanh-hidden, linear-output network with sum-of-squares error, derives its forward-pass quantities, output and hidden error signals, and gradients for both weight layers. Finally, it explains backpropagation's O(W) computational efficiency and contrasts it with forward and central finite-difference methods, including their approximation errors, roundoff limitations, doubled cost for central differences, and loss of linear scaling.

nodes.title: 5.3.3 Efficiency of backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text gives the output and hidden error signals and corresponding weight gradients for a two-layer neural network, then explains backpropagation's O(W) efficiency compared with finite-difference methods, which have O(W²) cost despite central differences improving accuracy. Numerical differentiation is recommended for implementation checks, while backpropagation is preferred for training. It also introduces the Jacobian of network outputs with respect to inputs and shows how Jacobians and the chain rule propagate derivatives and errors through differentiable modular systems.

nodes.title: 5.3.4 The Jacobian matrix
nodes.summary: The text explains how numerical differentiation is mainly used to verify, rather than replace, efficient backpropagation. It introduces the Jacobian as the matrix of output sensitivities to inputs, describes its use for modular networks, parameter-gradient propagation, and estimating output effects from small input errors, and derives a recursive backpropagation procedure for computing it, including sigmoid and softmax output cases and finite-difference validation. It then introduces the Hessian of the error with respect to weights and biases, outlining its roles in second-order training, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian Laplace approximations, and notes that it can be computed exactly through an extension of backpropagation.

This section explains error backpropagation as the efficient forward-and-backward evaluation of error-function derivatives, distinct from the optimization method used to update weights. It develops the chain-rule algorithm for general feed-forward networks, batch gradient accumulation, activation-specific units, and a detailed two-layer example, while establishing its O(W) efficiency. It contrasts backpropagation with finite-difference checks, then extends derivative propagation to network Jacobians and introduces Hessians and their applications in second-order training, pruning, retraining, and Bayesian approximations. The surrounding discussion also compares on-line, batch, and mini-batch training, emphasizing redundancy handling and possible escape from local minima.

nodes.title: 5.4. The Hessian Matrix
5.4.1 Diagonal approximation
nodes.summary: The text discusses computationally efficient approximations to neural-network Hessians. It presents a diagonal approximation, including its recursive backpropagation evaluation, O(W) cost, exact-diagonal alternative, and the warning that strong nondiagonal structure can make it unreliable. It then derives the outer-product or Levenberg–Marquardt approximation for sum-of-squares regression, explains when the omitted residual-dependent term is negligible, gives its computational costs and validity conditions, and states the corresponding logistic cross-entropy and softmax forms. Exercises 5.16, 5.17, 5.19, and 5.20 are also listed.

nodes.title: 5.4.2 Outer product approximation
nodes.summary: The text derives the Hessian for a neural network using single-output sum-of-squares regression loss and explains the Levenberg–Marquardt or outer-product approximation obtained by dropping the residual-weighted second-derivative term. This is justified when predictions are accurate or when zero-mean residuals are uncorrelated with that term. The approximation is efficiently computed from first derivatives, but may fail for inadequately trained or general networks. Analogous weighted outer-product forms are given for sigmoid-output cross-entropy and softmax multiclass networks, and several exercises are referenced.

nodes.title: 5.4.3 Inverse Hessian
nodes.summary: The text presents two methods for obtaining Hessian information in neural networks. First, it uses an outer-product approximation and the Woodbury identity to update the inverse Hessian sequentially as data points are added, starting from a regularized matrix alpha I; the approach extends to multiple outputs and relates to quasi-Newton training methods. Second, it describes estimating Hessian elements through a four-point finite-difference formula, whose accuracy is limited by numerical precision and has a second-order truncation error.

nodes.title: 5.4.4 Finite differences
nodes.summary: The text presents three approaches to Hessian computation. An outer-product approximation enables a sequential inverse-Hessian update via the Woodbury identity, starting from alpha I and processing data points once; it also notes straightforward multi-output extension and quasi-Newton alternatives. Finite-difference methods compute second derivatives either directly from four error evaluations per element, costing O(W^3), or from backpropagated gradients, costing O(W^2), with central differences giving O(delta^2) accuracy. Finally, an exact backpropagation-based Hessian method is described for general differentiable feed-forward networks, with O(W^2) complexity, and the first Hessian block equations are introduced for a two-layer network.

nodes.title: 5.4.5 Exact evaluation of the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text compares numerical and exact methods for evaluating neural-network Hessians. Direct symmetric finite differences are second-order accurate but cost O(W³), whereas finite differences of backpropagated gradients cost O(W²). An exact backpropagation-based Hessian algorithm works for arbitrary differentiable feed-forward networks and also scales as O(W²); explicit block formulas are given for a two-layer network, including treatment of biases and skip connections. It then introduces efficient direct computation of Hessian-vector products, avoiding explicit O(W²) Hessian storage and aiming for O(W) computation by applying the operator R = vᵀ∇ to forward- and backpropagation equations.

nodes.title: 5.4.6 Fast multiplication by the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text completes formulas for neural-network Hessian elements, including treatment of biases and skip connections, then develops Pearlmutter's efficient O(W) method for computing Hessian-vector products by applying the operator R{·} = v^T∇ to standard forward- and backpropagation equations. It gives the resulting forward, backward, and gradient-product equations, discusses implementation and recovery of the full Hessian via unit vectors, and introduces regularization as a way to control neural-network complexity. The number of hidden units M affects parameter count and the underfitting-overfitting tradeoff, but local minima make validation-based selection across initializations useful; alternatively, a larger network can be controlled with a quadratic regularization term.

This section defines the neural-network Hessian and surveys its uses in second-order training, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian inference. It presents diagonal and outer-product/Levenberg–Marquardt approximations, their backpropagation-based computation, assumptions, costs, and limitations, including classification-specific forms. It explains sequential inverse-Hessian updates through the Woodbury identity, finite-difference alternatives and their accuracy and complexity, and exact O(W^2) Hessian backpropagation for general networks with biases and skip connections. Finally, it develops Pearlmutter’s efficient O(W) Hessian-vector products, discusses reconstructing or avoiding the full Hessian, and relates regularization and hidden-layer size to model complexity and overfitting.

nodes.title: 5.5. Regularization in Neural Networks
5.5.1 Consistent Gaussian priors
nodes.summary: The text discusses neural-network regularization through weight decay and early stopping. L2 weight decay controls model complexity and corresponds to a Gaussian weight prior, but ordinary treatment of all weights and biases is not invariant to linear rescaling and shifting of inputs and outputs. A layer-specific weight penalty provides consistency under these transformations, while its associated prior is improper unless separate bias priors are added. The framework can be generalized to grouped weight priors, with input-based grouping leading to automatic relevance determination. Early stopping controls complexity by halting iterative training at the minimum validation error, before overfitting increases, and is interpreted as limiting the growth of effective model degrees of freedom. The text also describes figures demonstrating hidden-unit model fits, local-minimum effects, and validation-based stopping.

nodes.title: 5.5.2 Early stopping
nodes.summary: The text discusses structured priors and regularization, explaining their transformation properties, the problems caused by improper priors with unconstrained biases, the use of separate bias hyperparameters, grouped weight priors, and automatic relevance determination. It then presents early stopping as a complexity-control method, describing validation-based stopping, its connection to effective degrees of freedom and weight decay, and the quantitative role of τη. Finally, it introduces input invariances in pattern recognition, explains why learning them from transformed examples can be impractical, and begins outlining four approaches, first describing training-set augmentation.

nodes.title: 5.5.3 Invariances
nodes.summary: The text discusses early stopping as a way to control the growing effective model complexity and select the iteration with minimum validation error, noting its similarity to weight decay. It then explains input invariance requirements, including image translation and scale invariance and speech time-warp invariance, and presents four strategies: transformed-data augmentation, regularization, invariant preprocessing features, and invariant network or kernel architectures. Augmentation is flexible and improves generalization but can be costly; invariant features can extrapolate but may lose discriminative information. Finally, it introduces tangent propagation, which regularizes a model to remain unchanged along manifolds generated by continuous input transformations, with accompanying illustrations of stopping, weight decay, and digit warping.

nodes.title: 5.5.4 Tangent propagation
nodes.summary: The text discusses synthetic image warping and the limitations of hand-crafted invariant features, then develops tangent propagation as a Jacobian-based regularization method for enforcing local invariance to continuous transformations. It defines transformation manifolds and tangent vectors, derives the output derivative and regularized error, explains finite-difference tangent estimation, multi-parameter and combined transformations, and relates the idea to tangent distance. It finally introduces training with transformed data, showing its connection to tangent propagation and stating the expected sum-of-squares error formulation before beginning the transformed-data analysis.

nodes.title: 5.5.5 Training with transformed data
nodes.summary: The text connects tangent distance, transformation-based data augmentation, tangent propagation, and regularization as methods for achieving transformation invariance. It derives that training on small, zero-mean transformed inputs adds a tangent-based regularizer to the loss, which reduces to tangent propagation and, for additive noise, to Tikhonov regularization related to noise-based generalization improvements. It then introduces convolutional networks as an architectural approach to invariance, motivated by the local pixel correlations and hierarchical feature structure of images, especially handwritten digits subject to translations, scaling, rotations, and elastic deformations.

nodes.title: 5.5.6 Convolutional networks
nodes.summary: The text explains that small input transformations lead to a gradient-based regularizer, which becomes Tikhonov regularization for additive noise and is related to improved generalization. It then introduces convolutional neural networks as architectures that encode image invariances through local receptive fields, shared weights, and subsampling, describing feature maps, convolution, pooling-like subsampling, stacked layers, training, and parameter reduction. Finally, it introduces soft weight sharing, in which weight groups are encouraged rather than forced to have equal values, with their grouping and statistical properties learned from data.

nodes.title: 5.5.7 Soft weight sharing
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of convolutional networks and regularization, explaining feature maps, subsampling, translation invariance, layered architecture, backpropagation with shared weights, and parameter reduction. It then presents soft weight sharing, which regularizes weights through a learnable Gaussian mixture model rather than forcing exact equality. The mixture-based objective, posterior responsibilities, and derivatives for weights, means, variances, and mixing coefficients are given, along with positivity and normalization parameterizations. Finally, it introduces mixture density networks for modeling multimodal conditional distributions, using robot-arm inverse kinematics and other inverse problems to explain why ordinary Gaussian regression may fail, and starts describing a toy multimodal dataset.

The section concludes the Hessian-vector propagation discussion and then surveys neural-network regularization and complexity control. It covers hidden-unit selection, weight decay and consistent Gaussian or grouped priors, automatic relevance determination, early stopping, and several strategies for enforcing input invariances, including augmentation, invariant features, tangent propagation, and transformed-data training. It derives the relationship between transformation-based training, Jacobian penalties, and Tikhonov regularization, then presents convolutional architectures with shared weights and subsampling as structural invariance mechanisms. Finally, it develops soft weight sharing through learnable Gaussian mixtures and introduces mixture density networks for multimodal regression and inverse problems.

nodes.title: 5.6. Mixture Density Networks
nodes.summary: The text introduces mixture density networks as a solution to multimodal and heteroscedastic conditional prediction problems, using robot-arm inverse kinematics and a toy forward/inverse data set to show why Gaussian least-squares regression can fail. A neural network outputs the parameters of an input-dependent Gaussian mixture: softmax mixing coefficients, positive variances obtained by exponentiation, and unrestricted component means. The model is trained by maximum likelihood and differentiated through responsibilities that provide backpropagation error signals. It can represent conditional densities that change between unimodal and multimodal forms, from which means, variances, and approximate modes can be derived; the conditional mean recovers standard least-squares regression but may be inappropriate for multimodal targets. The text then begins Bayesian neural networks, contrasting maximum-likelihood and MAP estimation with Bayesian marginalization over weights, noting that exact inference is generally impossible for multilayer networks because of nonconvex posteriors, motivating variational factorized-Gaussian approximations.

nodes.title: 5.7. Bayesian Neural Networks
5.7.1 Posterior parameter distribution
nodes.summary: This section develops Bayesian neural-network regression using a Laplace approximation and a local linearization of the network around its MAP weights. It specifies Gaussian likelihood and weight-prior models, derives the approximate Gaussian posterior from the posterior Hessian, and obtains an analytical Gaussian predictive distribution whose variance combines observation noise with parameter uncertainty. It then applies the evidence framework to estimate the hyperparameters alpha and beta and compare network models, presenting the approximate log evidence, regularized error, and the eigenvalue-based effective-parameter formulation used to optimize alpha.

nodes.title: 5.7.2 Hyperparameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text describes Bayesian neural-network regression predictions as Gaussian, combining intrinsic noise with input-dependent parameter uncertainty. It then develops evidence-based optimization of the weight-prior and noise hyperparameters α and β using a Laplace approximation, giving the approximate log evidence, regularized error, Hessian-eigenvalue effective parameter count, and iterative re-estimation formulas. It discusses limitations caused by nonlinear Hessian dependence, posterior multimodality, initialization sensitivity, equivalent and inequivalent weight solutions, evidence-based model comparison, the numerical difficulty of Hessian determinants, and symmetry correction factors for hidden units. Finally, it introduces the subsequent treatment of Bayesian neural networks for classification.

nodes.title: 5.7.3 Bayesian neural networks for classification
nodes.summary: The text completes the evidence-based Laplace treatment of Bayesian neural-network regression, giving effective-parameter and noise-precision re-estimation formulas, explaining the need for iterative hyperparameter/posterior updates, multimodal solutions and hidden-unit symmetries, and practical issues in evaluating model evidence and Hessian determinants. It then develops the corresponding binary-classification method: Bernoulli likelihood without β, Gaussian prior controlled by α, MAP training with regularization, Hessian-based posterior approximation, evidence optimization, and predictive inference. Classification predictions are first approximated at the MAP weights and then improved by linearizing the sigmoid preactivation, deriving its Gaussian uncertainty, and applying a sigmoid-Gaussian approximation; examples show reduced overfitting and less confident predictions. The text concludes with exercises on converting sigmoid hidden units to tanh units and relating Gaussian-output likelihood maximization to sum-of-squares minimization.

The section finishes the discussion of mixture density networks by deriving their input-dependent variance and explaining why a most-probable mixture component can be preferable to a conditional mean for multimodal targets. It then introduces Bayesian neural networks, contrasting maximum-likelihood or MAP parameter estimation with Bayesian marginalization, and explains why nonlinear, nonconvex neural-network posteriors require approximations. Laplace-based Bayesian regression is developed using Gaussian likelihoods and priors, local linearization, Gaussian predictive distributions, and evidence-based optimization of alpha and beta through Hessian eigenvalues and effective parameter counts. The section discusses iterative optimization, model comparison, multimodality, initialization, symmetries, and determinant-computation difficulties. It extends the treatment to binary classification with Bernoulli likelihoods, MAP regularization, Laplace posteriors, evidence optimization, and uncertainty-aware sigmoid predictions, including examples and related exercises.

nodes.title: 5.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of Laplace approximations for Bayesian neural networks, explaining an approximation for the otherwise intractable Gaussian–logistic convolution and illustrating how parameter marginalization makes predictions less confident without changing the decision boundary. It then presents exercises covering sigmoid–tanh network equivalence, likelihood and error-function derivations for regression and classification, correlated Gaussian targets and covariance estimation, robustness to label noise, cross-entropy and output-unit derivatives, tanh differentiation, alternative binary target encoding, and the eigenvalue criterion for Hessian positive definiteness.

nodes.title: 5.5 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 5.3–5.10 cover maximum-likelihood estimation for multivariate Gaussian regression with known or unknown coupled covariance, robust binary classification under label noise, the equivalence of multiclass maximum likelihood and cross-entropy minimization, derivatives for sigmoid and softmax output units, the tanh derivative, reformulation of binary classification for bipolar targets and outputs, and the eigenvalue criterion for Hessian positive definiteness.

nodes.title: 5.6 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 5.3–5.10 on neural-network likelihoods, classification error functions, activation derivatives, and Hessian definiteness. It covers multivariate Gaussian regression with known or learned covariance, robust binary classification under label noise, the equivalence of maximum likelihood and cross-entropy for multiclass networks, derivative identities for sigmoid and softmax outputs, the tanh derivative, reformulation of binary classification with ±1 targets, and the eigenvalue criterion for positive-definite Hessian matrices.

nodes.title: 5.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 5.3–5.10 cover maximum-likelihood errors for multivariate Gaussian regression with known or learned covariance, robust binary classification with label noise, the equivalence of likelihood maximization and cross-entropy minimization for multiclass networks, derivatives of logistic-sigmoid, softmax, and tanh activations, reformulation of binary classification for targets ±1, and the eigenvalue characterization of positive-definite Hessian matrices.

nodes.title: 5.10 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 5.3–5.10 address maximum-likelihood error functions for multivariate Gaussian regression and noisy binary classification, including covariance estimation and robustness to label errors; the equivalence of likelihood maximization and cross-entropy minimization for multiclass networks; derivatives of logistic-sigmoid and softmax cross-entropy losses; the tanh derivative; reformulation of binary classification for outputs and targets in [-1, 1]; and the eigenvalue characterization of positive-definite Hessian matrices.

nodes.title: 5.11 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on quadratic error geometry and optimization, including elliptical error contours, the Hessian positive-definiteness criterion for local minima, and counting independent quadratic-form parameters. It also covers Taylor-expansion cancellation, forward-propagation methods for computing neural-network Jacobians, extensions of the Hessian outer-product approximation to multiple outputs and cross-entropy losses, a theoretical derivation of the Hessian for squared expected loss, and derivative equations for networks with direct input-to-output skip connections.

nodes.title: 5.12 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on quadratic error geometry and optimization, including elliptical error contours determined by Hessian eigenvectors and eigenvalues, the positive-definiteness condition for local minima, and the number of independent quadratic-form parameters. It also asks for a Taylor-series cancellation check, a forward-propagation derivation of neural-network Jacobians, extensions of the Hessian outer-product approximation to multiple outputs and logistic cross-entropy networks, a derivation of the expected Hessian for squared loss using conditional expectations, and derivative equations for networks with direct input-to-output skip connections.

nodes.title: 5.17 ( ) Consider a squared loss function of the form
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on quadratic error surfaces, requiring derivations of elliptical Hessian-aligned contours, the positive-definiteness condition for local minima, and the number of independent quadratic-error parameters. It also asks for Taylor-expansion verification, a forward-propagation method for computing neural-network Jacobians, extensions of the Hessian outer-product approximation to multiple outputs and logistic cross-entropy networks, a probabilistic derivation of the Hessian for squared loss, and derivative equations for skip-layer connections.

nodes.title: 5.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 5.11–5.41 develop neural-network optimization, curvature, differentiation, regularization, invariances, mixture-density modeling, robot kinematics, and Bayesian inference. They cover eigenvalue analysis of quadratic errors; Hessian definiteness, parameter counting, and Taylor expansions; forward and backward Jacobian/Hessian computations for single and multiple outputs, skip connections, logistic, softmax, and cross-entropy models; exact and outer-product curvature updates; early stopping as regularization; tangent propagation, noise-induced Tikhonov regularization, and tied-weight backpropagation; softmax derivatives; mixture-density-network gradients and moments; and Laplace-approximation predictive distributions, evidence, and multiclass Bayesian neural-network extensions.

This section presents multilayer perceptrons as adaptive nonlinear models for regression and classification, covering their architectures, activations, forward computation, approximation properties, symmetries, and probabilistic interpretations. It develops maximum-likelihood objectives for Gaussian, Bernoulli, and softmax outputs and examines the challenges of nonconvex training, optimization algorithms, initialization, validation, curvature, and error backpropagation. The section then treats Jacobians, Hessians, second-order methods, Hessian approximations and Hessian-vector products, followed by regularization through priors, weight decay, sparsity, early stopping, invariance methods, convolutional structures, and soft weight sharing. It introduces mixture density networks for multimodal conditional distributions and concludes with Bayesian neural networks, Laplace approximations, evidence, predictive uncertainty, and classification extensions. Exercises reinforce likelihoods, derivatives, optimization geometry, Hessian and Jacobian calculations, skip connections, regularization, mixture models, and Bayesian inference.

nodes.title: 6 Kernel Methods
6.1. Dual Representations
nodes.summary: The text develops the dual formulation of regularized linear least-squares regression. It shows that the weight vector is a combination of training feature vectors, rewrites the objective using the Gram matrix, derives a = (K + λI)^−1t, and expresses predictions solely through kernel evaluations and training targets. Although the dual requires an N × N inversion rather than an M × M one, it avoids explicit feature representations and enables implicit use of high- or infinite-dimensional spaces. The text then introduces kernel construction both from feature mappings and directly, emphasizing that valid kernels must represent inner products, with (x^Tz)^2 as an example.

nodes.title: 6.2. Constructing Kernels
Techniques for Constructing New Kernels.
nodes.summary: The text presents rules for constructing valid kernels and emphasizes that kernels must be symmetric, positive semidefinite, and application-appropriate. It discusses polynomial and Gaussian kernels, including their feature representations and generalized forms, then extends kernel methods to symbolic objects such as sets. It explains how probabilistic generative models, mixtures, latent variables, hidden Markov models, and Fisher scores can define kernels, including sequence and document applications. The sigmoidal kernel is noted as a commonly used but generally invalid positive-semidefinite kernel, alongside its relationship to neural networks and Gaussian processes. The section then introduces radial basis function networks, describing distance-based basis functions, exact interpolation, overfitting with noisy data, and their connection to regularization theory and Green’s functions.

This section explains how kernel methods replace explicit feature mappings with inner products and how valid kernels can be constructed. It gives feature-map and direct-construction examples, including polynomial kernels and their nonlinear representations, and states the Gram-matrix positive-semidefiniteness criterion. It then presents closure-based kernel construction and applications to numerical and symbolic data, probabilistic models, sequences, and documents, while discussing the limitations of sigmoidal kernels. Finally, it introduces radial basis function networks, covering interpolation, noise-related overfitting, and their relationship to regularization and Green's functions.

nodes.title: 6.3. Radial Basis Function Networks
6.3.1 Nadaraya-Watson model
nodes.summary: The text discusses methods for selecting radial-basis-function centres and then develops the Nadaraya-Watson kernel-regression model from Parzen density estimation. It derives the normalized kernel-weighted prediction and its summation constraint, explains that the model provides a full conditional distribution, and illustrates Gaussian-kernel regression and uncertainty on sinusoidal data. Extensions using more flexible Gaussian components and Gaussian mixture models are described, including their trade-off between training and prediction cost, before introducing Gaussian processes.

This section explains radial basis function networks as linear models whose basis functions depend on distance from centres. It covers their origins in exact interpolation, regularization and noisy-input modeling, derives normalized radial bases and the Nadaraya–Watson kernel-regression model, and explains the benefits of normalization. To reduce prediction cost, it discusses using fewer data-selected centres with least-squares coefficients. The subsection develops the Nadaraya–Watson model from Parzen density estimation, including normalized kernel predictions, conditional uncertainty, Gaussian-kernel examples, more flexible Gaussian and mixture models, their computational trade-offs, and the transition to Gaussian processes.

nodes.title: 6.4. Gaussian Processes
6.4.1 Linear regression revisited
nodes.summary: The text introduces Gaussian processes as Bayesian, nonparametric priors over functions and explains that finite data require only finite-dimensional Gaussian distributions. It derives a Gaussian process from Bayesian linear regression with Gaussian weight priors, showing that the induced function-value covariance is a kernel or Gram matrix, and defines general Gaussian processes through their mean and covariance functions. Gaussian, exponential, and related stochastic-process kernels are discussed, along with connections to kriging, ARMA models, Kalman filters, radial basis networks, and Gaussian random fields. The text then extends Gaussian processes to regression by adding independent Gaussian observation noise, specifying the latent-function prior and likelihood, explaining kernel-based similarity, and integrating out the latent values to obtain the marginal Gaussian distribution of observed targets.

nodes.title: 6.4.2 Gaussian processes for regression
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian-process regression by adding independent Gaussian observation noise to a Gaussian-process prior over latent function values. Integrating the latent values gives a Gaussian marginal distribution whose covariance is the kernel covariance plus noise variance. It presents a quadratic-exponential kernel with constant and linear components, illustrates prior sampling and regression conditioning, and derives the predictive mean and variance through Gaussian conditioning. The predictive mean is a kernel, or radial-basis, expansion, subject to positive-semidefinite kernel requirements. The text compares Gaussian-process and finite-basis linear-regression computation, notes the ability of Gaussian processes to represent infinite-basis models and the need for large-data approximations, and mentions extensions to multiple outputs, manifolds, and stochastic differential equations. It then explains hyperparameter learning through marginal-likelihood maximization and its gradients, discusses nonconvexity, priors, and approximate Bayesian marginalization, and introduces the need for input-dependent noise models in heteroscedastic regression.

nodes.title: 6.4.3 Learning the hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text discusses Gaussian process applications, learning covariance-function hyperparameters through likelihood maximization and gradient optimization, the associated likelihood and gradient formulas, nonconvexity and Bayesian treatment of hyperparameters, and extensions for input-dependent noise using a second Gaussian process. It then introduces automatic relevance determination, explaining how separate kernel precision parameters reveal the importance of individual inputs, with illustrative prior samples and a synthetic-data example.

nodes.title: 6.4.4 Automatic relevance determination
nodes.summary: The text introduces input-dependent variance modeling in Gaussian processes and explains automatic relevance determination, which uses separate kernel precision parameters for each input to identify relevant and irrelevant variables through marginal-likelihood optimization. It presents the ARD kernel, prior-sample behavior, a three-variable synthetic demonstration, and an ARD extension of the exponential-quadratic kernel. It then begins Gaussian-process classification, explaining how a latent GP is transformed by a logistic sigmoid to produce binary-class probabilities.

nodes.title: 6.4.5 Gaussian processes for classification
nodes.summary: The text demonstrates ARD in Gaussian processes, showing that optimized input-specific hyperparameters identify informative, noisy, and irrelevant variables, and gives the corresponding ARD kernel. It then develops Gaussian-process classification by applying a logistic sigmoid to a latent Gaussian process, defining the Bernoulli likelihood, latent Gaussian prior, numerically stabilized covariance, and binary predictive probability. Because the required posterior integral is intractable, sampling and Gaussian-approximation methods are discussed, including variational inference, expectation propagation, and the Laplace approximation. Their motivations and properties are summarized, including variational likelihood bounds and multiclass extension, before the text begins deriving the Laplace posterior by marginalizing the training latent variables using Bayes’ theorem.

nodes.title: 6.4.6 Laplace approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains approximate inference for Gaussian-process classification, focusing on the Laplace approximation. It introduces the intractable predictive sigmoid integral, compares sampling, variational inference, expectation propagation, and Laplace methods, and derives the Laplace procedure: posterior mode finding through Newton-Raphson/IRLS, Hessian-based Gaussian approximation, predictive latent mean and variance, and approximate class probabilities. It also derives Laplace-approximated marginal likelihood and hyperparameter gradients, illustrates classification on synthetic data, notes multiclass extensions, and discusses the infinite-hidden-unit connection between Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, including the loss of output sharing and the resulting nonstationary kernels.

nodes.title: 6.4.7 Connection to neural networks
nodes.summary: The text explains the connection between Gaussian processes and infinitely wide Bayesian neural networks, including the loss of output sharing, the resulting nonstationary kernels, and the role of weight-prior hyperparameters. It also presents a Gaussian-process classification illustration and lists exercises on dual representations, perceptron and nearest-neighbour kernelization, positive-definite matrices, kernel-construction proofs, and a kernel tailored to a target function.

This section moves from kernel-density regression and its full conditional distributions to Gaussian processes as Bayesian nonparametric priors over functions. It derives Gaussian processes from Bayesian linear regression, defines their kernels and covariance functions, and develops noisy Gaussian-process regression, prediction, computational properties, extensions, and hyperparameter learning, including heteroscedastic noise. Automatic relevance determination identifies relevant inputs through separate kernel parameters. The section then develops Gaussian-process classification with sigmoid likelihoods and approximate inference methods, especially the Laplace approximation, covering prediction, marginal likelihood, optimization, and multiclass issues. It closes by relating Gaussian processes to infinitely wide Bayesian neural networks and includes related kernel and positive-definiteness exercises.

This section presents kernel methods as dual and nonparametric approaches that base prediction on similarities among training data rather than only learned parameter vectors. It introduces feature-space inner products, the kernel trick, kernel validity and construction, and dual regularized regression. It then develops radial basis networks and Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression, including interpolation, regularization, noisy inputs, normalization, Gaussian and mixture models, uncertainty, and computational reductions. The section culminates in Gaussian processes, covering their Bayesian-linear-regression foundations, covariance kernels, regression and classification, prediction, noise models, hyperparameter learning, automatic relevance determination, approximate inference, multiclass issues, and links to infinitely wide neural networks. The accompanying exercises address kernel feature representations, Fisher and subset kernels, positive definiteness and inequalities, representer results, noisy-input and mixture regression, Gaussian-process identities, and classification inference and optimization.

nodes.title: 7 Sparse Kernel Machines
7.1. Maximum Margin Classifiers
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
nodes.summary: The text derives the kernelized dual formulation of the maximum-margin classifier, including its quadratic-programming constraints, computational implications, positive-definite kernel requirement, and prediction rule. KKT conditions identify the sparse set of support vectors, explain their geometric role, and provide a stable method for estimating the bias term. The classifier is also expressed using an infinite-penalty error function and quadratic regularization. A Gaussian-kernel example demonstrates nonlinear separation and sparsity. The section then introduces overlapping class distributions and slack variables, allowing margin violations and misclassifications with penalties proportional to their distance beyond the margin.

nodes.title: 7.1.1 Overlapping class distributions
nodes.summary: The text explains soft-margin SVMs for overlapping classes, introducing slack variables and the parameter C to trade off margin size against violations and errors. It derives the Lagrangian, KKT conditions, dual quadratic program, support-vector interpretation, and bias estimation, then presents the ν-SVM and its interpretation. It discusses efficient training through chunking, decomposition, and SMO; clarifies why kernels do not avoid dimensionality issues using a polynomial-kernel example; and describes converting SVM scores into approximate probabilities with Platt scaling, including its independence and calibration limitations. The section concludes by beginning a comparison between nonseparable SVMs and logistic regression.

nodes.title: 7.1.2 Relation to logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text explains that polynomial kernels may use a higher-dimensional feature representation while restricting inputs to a lower-dimensional nonlinear manifold. It then discusses converting nonprobabilistic SVM outputs into probabilities through Platt's sigmoid calibration and warns about overfitting and poor calibration. SVMs for nonseparable data are reformulated as regularized hinge-loss minimization and compared with logistic and squared-error objectives, emphasizing that hinge loss yields sparse solutions. Finally, it reviews multiclass SVM strategies, including one-versus-the-rest, modified target coding, and joint optimization, along with their consistency, imbalance, and computational trade-offs.

nodes.title: 7.1.3 Multiclass SVMs
nodes.summary: The text compares classification error functions, noting that hinge loss promotes sparsity, logistic and hinge losses approximate misclassification error, and squared error can overemphasize confidently correct points. It then surveys multiclass SVM strategies: one-versus-the-rest and its variants, joint optimization, one-versus-one voting, DAGSVM, and error-correcting output codes, including their ambiguities, class imbalance, robustness, and computational costs. It also describes one-class SVMs for enclosing a specified high-density region using either a maximum-margin hyperplane or a minimum enclosing feature-space sphere, and concludes by introducing sparse SVM regression.

nodes.title: 7.1.4 SVMs for regression
nodes.summary: The text discusses multiclass and single-class SVMs, SVM regression, and the foundations of computational learning theory. Multiclass strategies include one-versus-one voting, its more efficient DAGSVM organization, and error-correcting output codes, while one-versus-the-rest remains most common. Single-class SVMs enclose high-density regions using either a separating hyperplane or a feature-space sphere. SVM regression uses epsilon-insensitive loss, slack variables, a kernelized constrained dual formulation, KKT conditions, and sparse support-vector predictions; a nu formulation controls the fractions of points outside the tube and serving as support vectors. Finally, PAC learning defines probabilistic generalization guarantees, and VC dimension measures hypothesis-space complexity for deriving sample-size bounds.

nodes.title: 7.1.5 Computational learning theory
nodes.summary: The text presents an illustration of ν-SVM regression, reviews computational/statistical learning theory through the PAC framework, expected-error and probability requirements, VC dimension, and the conservative nature of PAC and PAC-Bayesian bounds. It then introduces Relevance Vector Machines as Bayesian sparse kernel alternatives to SVMs that provide probabilistic outputs, greater sparsity, and faster prediction while avoiding several SVM limitations, beginning with their Gaussian-noise regression formulation.

The section develops support vector machines from maximum-margin classification for linearly separable data through dual kernel formulations, KKT-based support-vector sparsity, bias estimation, and nonlinear Gaussian-kernel examples. It extends the framework to overlapping classes with soft margins, slack penalties, C- and ν-SVMs, and efficient optimization methods; discusses kernel dimensionality and probability calibration; compares hinge loss with logistic and squared-error objectives; and surveys multiclass and one-class SVM strategies. It then covers epsilon-insensitive sparse SVM regression and ν-regression, places generalization in the context of PAC learning and VC dimension, and introduces Bayesian relevance vector machines as more-sparse probabilistic alternatives.

nodes.title: 7.2. Relevance Vector Machines
7.2.1 RVM for regression
nodes.summary: The text contrasts conservative PAC and PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds with the relevance vector machine, a Bayesian sparse-kernel alternative to SVMs. It develops RVM regression as Gaussian linear regression with kernel or arbitrary basis functions and separate weight precisions, explains evidence-based hyperparameter learning, posterior and predictive distributions, and automatic relevance determination that prunes weights and yields relevance vectors. It discusses predictive uncertainty and undesirable extrapolation overconfidence, illustrates the model’s greater sparsity and comparable accuracy relative to SVMs, and reviews its benefits, computational costs, nonconvex training disadvantage, and the transition to a detailed analysis of sparsity.

nodes.title: 7.2.2 Analysis of sparsity
Sequential Sparse Bayesian Learning Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how the RVM marginal likelihood’s quality and sparsity measures determine whether a basis vector is retained or pruned, derives the two possible optimal values of α_i, and illustrates them graphically. It then presents a sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm for adding, updating, or removing basis functions, gives efficient formulas for the required quantities and their computational complexity, and begins the extension of the RVM framework to binary classification using an ARD prior and logistic-sigmoid model.

This section analyzes how automatic relevance determination produces sparse RVMs: basis functions poorly aligned with the data are assigned infinite precision and pruned, as illustrated geometrically and formalized by decomposing the marginal likelihood into basis-specific sparsity and quality terms. It contrasts RVM compactness, prediction efficiency, automatic hyperparameter selection, and training costs with SVMs, then develops the sequential sparse Bayesian learning procedure for efficiently adding, updating, and removing basis functions, including optimal precision solutions, update formulas, and complexity considerations. It concludes by introducing the extension of RVMs to binary classification with ARD and a logistic-sigmoid model.

nodes.title: 7.2.3 RVM for classification
nodes.summary: The text completes the sparse Bayesian regression RVM update algorithm, defines efficient quality and sparseness calculations, and explains its O(M^3) active-basis complexity. It then develops binary RVM classification using a logistic model, ARD priors, IRLS, and a Laplace posterior approximation, deriving the posterior, marginal likelihood, and hyperparameter update and showing that the regression sparsity algorithm carries over. It discusses the location and probabilistic nature of relevance vectors, extends the method to multiclass softmax classification, and compares its computational costs and sparsity advantages with SVMs. The section concludes with exercises covering Parzen and feature-space nearest-mean classification, maximum-margin properties and dual relations, logistic-regression regularization, and derivation of the regression SVM dual.

This section develops relevance vector machines as sparse Bayesian alternatives to SVMs for regression and classification. It explains Gaussian and logistic formulations, ARD-based evidence optimization, posterior and predictive inference, uncertainty, relevance-vector sparsity, marginal-likelihood analysis, and sequential sparse Bayesian learning. It covers computational complexity, training disadvantages, extrapolation behavior, comparisons with SVMs, binary and multiclass extensions, and exercises on related classification, regularization, maximum-margin, and duality concepts.
