nodes.title: 8 Graphical Models
8.1. Bayesian Networks
8.1.1 Example: Polynomial regression
nodes.summary: The text explains how directed acyclic graphs represent and factorize joint probability distributions, including the parent-conditioned product rule, normalization, and the acyclicity requirement. It applies these ideas to Bayesian polynomial regression, introducing repeated-node plates, explicit deterministic parameters, observed and latent variables, posterior inference for coefficients, and predictive inference for new inputs by integrating out the coefficients. It concludes by describing ancestral sampling from a DAG and obtaining marginal samples by discarding unneeded sampled variables.

nodes.title: 8.1.2 Generative models
nodes.summary: The text explains parameter-marginalized prediction and introduces ancestral sampling for directed graphical models, including node ordering, conditional sampling, and extraction of marginals. It describes generative models in which latent variables explain observed data, illustrates this with object images governed by identity, position, and orientation, contrasts generative models with polynomial regression, and explains the use of synthetic samples for model interpretation. It then introduces discrete variables as a continuation of the discussion of exponential-family distributions.

nodes.title: 8.1.3 Discrete variables
nodes.summary: The text explains how graphical models represent observations and latent variables, using an object-recognition example in which object identity, position, and orientation generate an image. It distinguishes generative models, which encode data-generation processes and support ancestral sampling of synthetic observations, from nongenerative models such as ordinary polynomial regression without an input prior. It then introduces discrete variables in Bayesian networks: multinomial nodes require K − 1 parameters, unrestricted joint distributions over M K-state variables require K^M − 1, and graph structure reduces complexity by imposing conditional independencies. Independent graphs need M(K − 1) parameters, while a discrete chain grows linearly with its length; parameter tying reduces this further. Dirichlet priors provide Bayesian versions of these models. Finally, the text describes replacing exponentially large conditional-probability tables with parameterized logistic-sigmoid conditionals, reducing the number of parameters for a binary child with many binary parents from exponential to linear growth at the cost of a more restricted distribution.

nodes.title: 8.1.4 Linear-Gaussian models
nodes.summary: The text develops linear-Gaussian graphical models, showing how Gaussian conditionals with linear parent dependencies produce a multivariate Gaussian joint distribution and how its mean and covariance are computed recursively. It analyzes independent, fully connected, and partially connected graphs, including a three-node example, then generalizes the construction to vector-valued Gaussian nodes and connects it to conjugate priors, hyperpriors, and hierarchical Bayesian models. It concludes by defining conditional independence and demonstrating its equivalent conditional factorization property.

This section introduces Bayesian networks as directed acyclic graphical models that factor joint distributions into node-conditioned probabilities, explaining parent-child structure, ordering, normalization, fully connected graphs, and the significance of missing links. It applies the framework to polynomial regression and generative modeling, covering latent and observed variables, plates, posterior and predictive inference, parameter marginalization, ancestral sampling, and synthetic-data interpretation. It then treats discrete networks, showing how graph structure, parameter tying, Dirichlet priors, and logistic conditional models control parameter complexity. Finally, it develops linear-Gaussian networks, including scalar and vector-valued cases, recursive Gaussian moments, graph structures, conjugate and hierarchical Bayesian extensions, and the relationship between conditional independence and factorization.

nodes.title: 8.2. Conditional Independence
8.2.1 Three example graphs
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional independence and explains why it is useful in probabilistic graphical models. Through three three-node directed graphs, it contrasts tail-to-tail, head-to-tail, and head-to-head paths: conditioning on a common cause or intermediate node blocks dependence, whereas conditioning on a common effect creates dependence, including through descendants. A numerical battery, fuel-tank, and gauge example demonstrates explaining away. The section then states the general d-separation criterion: paths are blocked by observed non-collider nodes or unobserved colliders without observed descendants, and if all paths between two node sets are blocked by a conditioning set, the corresponding conditional independence is implied by the graph.

nodes.title: 8.2.2 D-separation
nodes.summary: The text explains explaining away through a fuel-gauge and battery example, showing how conditioning can induce dependence and alter posterior probabilities. It then defines d-separation for directed acyclic graphs, including the path-blocking rules for observed non-colliders and unobserved colliders, and illustrates these rules with graph examples and parameter nodes. Applications include conditional independence in i.i.d. Gaussian data with a latent mean, Bayesian polynomial regression, and the naive Bayes classifier, whose assumptions, Gaussian interpretation, uses, and limitations are discussed. The d-separation theorem is presented as equivalent to the directed factorization property, with graphs viewed as filters over families of distributions and examples ranging from fully connected to fully disconnected graphs. The section concludes with the Markov blanket—parents, children, and co-parents—and introduces undirected Markov random fields as graphical models whose independencies are based on ordinary graph separation.

This section develops conditional independence in graphical models, beginning with multivariate linear-Gaussian and hierarchical Bayesian constructions. It defines conditional independence and explains how graph structures determine dependence, independence, and explaining-away effects through d-separation. The discussion covers path-blocking rules, applications to Gaussian latent-variable models, polynomial regression, and naive Bayes, the equivalence of d-separation with directed factorization, and the interpretation of graphs as independence constraints. It concludes with Markov blankets and an introduction to undirected Markov random fields.

nodes.title: 8.3. Markov Random Fields
8.3.1 Conditional independence properties
nodes.summary: The text explains directed-graph Markov blankets and then introduces Markov random fields as undirected graphical models that encode both factorization and conditional independence. In undirected graphs, A is conditionally independent of B given C when C separates them by lying on every connecting path, equivalently when removing C leaves no A-to-B path. This avoids the complications of explaining away in directed graphs. A node’s Markov blanket is simply its neighbors. The section then turns toward determining the corresponding local factorization of the joint distribution.

nodes.title: 8.3.2 Factorization properties
nodes.summary: The text explains conditional independence and factorization in undirected graphical models. Independence is determined by graph separation: all paths between A and B must pass through C, or equivalently C can be removed without leaving an A-to-B path. This avoids the directional and explaining-away issues of directed graphs. A node’s Markov blanket is simply its neighbors. The text then introduces cliques and maximal cliques, showing that undirected joint distributions factorize into nonnegative potential functions over maximal cliques, divided by a partition function for normalization. Unlike directed-graph factors, potentials need not be probabilities, and computing the partition function may be exponentially difficult, though it cancels for local conditionals and can be bypassed for suitably small marginals. Under strictly positive potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem establishes equivalence between graph-separation independencies and clique factorization. Potentials can be represented exponentially using energy functions, with global probabilities reflecting the balance of local configuration preferences. Finally, binary image denoising is introduced as an application, modeling noisy and clean ±1-valued pixels, random sign flips, and correlations between corresponding and neighboring pixels.

nodes.title: 8.3.3 Illustration: Image de-noising
nodes.summary: The passage establishes the equivalence, for positive distributions, between conditional independencies read by separation in an undirected graph and factorization over maximal cliques, then introduces energy/Boltzmann representations and explains the interpretive role of undirected potentials. It applies these ideas to binary image de-noising with an Ising-style Markov random field, specifying observation, neighbor, and bias energies, the resulting joint and conditional distributions, and the ICM optimization procedure, including its local-optimum limitation and example performance. It also contrasts ICM with max-product and globally optimal graph-cut methods, and begins explaining how a directed chain can be represented as an undirected chain with pairwise clique potentials.

nodes.title: 8.3.4 Relation to directed graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes an image-denoising discussion by contrasting ICM, max-product, and graph-cut optimization, noting local versus global maxima and the conditions under which graph cuts guarantee the global solution. It then explains how directed graphical models can be converted into undirected ones: conditional factors become clique potentials, and moralization connects co-parents before dropping directions, preserving the necessary factor scopes but potentially losing independencies. The text defines D maps, I maps, and perfect maps; compares the conditional-independence expressiveness of directed and undirected graphs through three- and four-variable examples; introduces chain graphs as a broader mixed framework; and begins the topic of inference, where observed nodes are used to compute posterior distributions efficiently through graphical structure.

This section develops Markov random fields as undirected graphical models whose separation properties encode conditional independence and whose distributions factorize over maximal cliques. It explains clique potentials, partition functions, the Hammersley–Clifford theorem, and energy representations, then applies them to binary image denoising with an Ising-style model and compares ICM, max-product, and graph-cut optimization. It also relates directed and undirected graphs through moralization, discusses independence-map relationships, expressive differences, and chain graphs, and introduces inference using graphical structure.

nodes.title: 8.4. Inference in Graphical Models
8.4.1 Inference on a chain
nodes.summary: The text introduces exact inference in graphical models through Bayes’ theorem and local message propagation. It derives efficient sum-product inference on an undirected chain, contrasting exponential naive marginalization with O(NK²) recursive computation using forward and backward messages. It explains normalization, computation of all node marginals, handling observed variables, and recovery of neighboring-node or clique marginals. These results are connected to Markov chains and Chapman–Kolmogorov equations and to EM-based parameter learning, before transitioning to inference on trees.

nodes.title: 8.4.2 Trees
nodes.summary: The text explains how bidirectional message passing efficiently computes every marginal in a chain, including handling observed variables by clamping, evaluating the normalization constant once, and obtaining neighboring-variable and clique-scope joint distributions. These local joints support EM parameter learning with missing data. It then generalizes exact message-passing inference from chains to trees, defining undirected trees, directed rooted trees, and polytrees and describing their relationships through moralization. Finally, it introduces factor graphs as an explicit variable-and-factor representation of joint distributions factored as products of functions over variable subsets, which provides a general form for the sum-product algorithm.

nodes.title: 8.4.3 Factor graphs
nodes.summary: The text explains why tree-structured graphs support efficient exact inference through local message passing and introduces factor graphs as a general bipartite representation of products of factors. It defines undirected trees, directed trees, and directed polytrees; describes their relationships under conversion and moralization; and shows how directed and undirected factorizations become factor graphs. Examples demonstrate that factor graphs preserve explicit factorization details, allow multiple equivalent representations, and retain tree structure even for polytrees where moralization creates loops. The section then sets up the sum-product algorithm for computing discrete local marginals, noting its extension to integration in linear-Gaussian models and to max-sum inference for most-probable states.

nodes.title: 8.4.4 The sum-product algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how factor graphs unify inference in directed and undirected tree-like graphical models, emphasizing that they can retain tree structure and represent factorizations without necessarily implying conditional independencies. It derives the sum-product algorithm for exact marginal inference: factor-to-variable messages combine a local factor with incoming messages and sum over other variables, while variable-to-factor messages multiply incoming messages from all other factors. Leaf initialization, recursive propagation, computation of all variable and factor marginals, message complexity, normalization for undirected models, and a four-variable worked example are presented. The method is extended to observed variables through indicator functions and to continuous models by replacing sums with integrals. Finally, the text introduces max-sum as a dynamic-programming alternative for finding the globally most probable joint assignment, contrasting it with independently maximizing individual marginals.

nodes.title: 8.4.5 The max-sum algorithm
nodes.summary: This section introduces max-sum, the dynamic-programming counterpart to sum-product for finding both the maximum joint probability and a jointly maximizing variable assignment. It explains why marginal maximization is insufficient, derives max-product and its logarithmic max-sum form using distributivity, gives message-update and initialization rules for chains and tree factor graphs, and describes root optimization, tie handling, backpointers, and backtracking for obtaining a consistent global configuration. The method is exact on trees, underlies the Viterbi algorithm for hidden Markov models, handles evidence by clamping observed variables, and is contrasted with the simpler but non-global ICM algorithm.

nodes.title: 8.4.6 Exact inference in general graphs
nodes.summary: The text outlines exact inference in loopy graphical models via the junction tree algorithm: moralizing directed graphs, triangulating them, constructing a maximum-spanning join tree of maximal cliques, condensing it into a junction tree with the running intersection property, and performing sum-product message passing to obtain marginals and conditionals. The method is exact but has cost exponential in the largest clique, characterized by the graph's treewidth. It then introduces loopy belief propagation as an approximate extension of sum-product to cyclic graphs, explaining its local message rules, possible convergence failure, initialization with unit messages, flooding and serial schedules, and the use of pending-message updates.

nodes.title: 8.4.7 Loopy belief propagation
nodes.summary: The text explains how junction-tree complexity is characterized by treewidth and why large treewidth limits exact inference. It then introduces loopy belief propagation as an approximate sum-product method for cyclic graphs, covering initialization, message updates, pending messages, flooding and serial schedules, convergence behavior, marginal computation, and applications to error-correcting codes. It also discusses learning graph structures from data, including Bayesian posterior scoring, computational challenges from latent-variable marginalization and the exponential structure space, and heuristic search. Two exercises concern normalization of directed-graph factorizations and the ordering characterization of acyclic directed graphs.

nodes.title: 8.4.8 Learning the graph structure
nodes.summary: The text explains termination and accuracy of belief propagation on trees, convergence and approximate marginals for loopy graphs, and its mixed performance including applications to error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graph structures from data, describing priors, posterior structure probabilities, model evidence, and the computational challenges of latent-variable marginalization and exponentially large structure spaces. Two exercises address normalization of directed-graph joint distributions and proving that an appropriate node ordering rules out directed cycles.

This section presents inference in graphical models, beginning with exact sum-product and max-sum message passing on chains, trees, and factor graphs, including evidence, normalization, local joint distributions, continuous variables, EM learning, and the Viterbi algorithm. It then extends exact inference to general graphs with junction trees and treewidth, and presents loopy belief propagation as an approximate method for cyclic graphs, including its schedules, convergence behavior, and coding applications. The section also discusses Bayesian learning of graph structures, latent-variable and search-related computational challenges, and includes exercises on factorization normalization and acyclic graph orderings.

nodes.title: 8.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text explains termination and accuracy of belief propagation on trees versus loopy graphs, computation of approximate marginals after convergence or stopping, and its variable performance, including success in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graphical-model structure, where candidate graphs are scored through their data evidence and posterior probabilities, while noting the computational challenges of latent-variable marginalization and exponentially large structure spaces. The exercises ask students to prove normalization of a directed-graph joint distribution and the connection between node ordering and absence of directed cycles.

nodes.title: 8.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of loopy belief propagation, contrasting exact termination and marginals on trees with possible nontermination and approximate results on loopy graphs, and noting its effectiveness in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graph structures, including posterior scoring by prior times model evidence and the computational difficulties of latent-variable marginalization and exponentially large structure spaces. The remainder presents Exercises 8.1–8.9 on normalization and acyclicity of directed graphical models, marginal and conditional independence using a specified binary distribution, directed-model factorization, relevance-vector-machine representation, the noisy-OR model, Gaussian recursion results, independence implications, and d-separation/Markov blankets.

nodes.title: 8.5 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 8.3–8.9 on probabilistic graphical models. They cover verifying marginal and conditional independence from a discrete joint table, deriving conditional distributions and a graph factorization, constructing a graphical model for a relevance vector machine, interpreting the noisy-OR model as a soft logical OR and explaining its baseline parameter, deriving Gaussian means and covariances via recursion, proving an implication between conditional-independence statements, and establishing the Markov-blanket conditional-independence property using d-separation.

nodes.title: 8.8 ( ) www Show that a ⊥⊥ b, c | d implies a ⊥⊥ b | d.
nodes.summary: The text presents a joint distribution table for three binary variables and exercises covering marginal and conditional independence, probability factorization and graph construction, graphical modeling of a relevance vector machine, interpretation of the noisy-OR model and its parameters, derivation of Gaussian means and covariances using recursion, properties of conditional independence, and the Markov-blanket conditional independence result proved via d-separation.

nodes.title: 8.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on discrete joint distributions, marginal and conditional independence, Bayesian-network factorization and graph construction, relevance-vector-machine graphical models, noisy-OR representations, Gaussian recursion, d-separation and Markov blankets, collider effects and explaining away, graph enumeration, local energy updates in ICM, maximum-probability configurations, and pairwise marginals in graphical models. It includes a binary-variable joint-distribution table, the noisy-OR formula, unreliable sensor-report probabilities, and references to several graphical-model figures and equations.

nodes.title: 8.12 ( ) www Show that there are 2 M(M−1)/2 distinct undirected graphs over a set of
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on graphical-model conditional independence, including the effect of observing a collider’s descendant and an unreliable fuel-gauge report; counting undirected graphs; locality of energy changes in iterated conditional modes; the maximum-probability configuration when interaction and bias coefficients vanish; and the joint distribution of neighboring nodes in a graph.

nodes.title: 8.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on d-separation and explaining away, including the effect of observing a descendant and an unreliable fuel-gauge report; counting undirected graphs; local energy differences and MAP configurations in ICM; distributions and inference in chain and tree graphical models; equivalence of directed and undirected trees; and the scheduling, correctness, and marginal calculations of the sum-product message-passing algorithm on tree-structured factor graphs.

nodes.title: 8.18 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 8.16–8.29 develop message passing and sum-product inference on directed and factor-tree graphs. They cover conditional inference with observed nodes, d-separation and independence, equivalence of directed and undirected tree models, recovery of chain-model formulas, valid message-passing orders, computation of variable, factor, and connected-subset marginals, alternative marginal identities, verification on a specific graph, joint inference by clamping variables, a counterexample involving marginal modes versus joint probability, and the behavior of pending messages: cycles prevent their complete elimination, whereas finite tree graphs eventually have none.

This section introduces probabilistic graphical models as visual tools for representing probability distributions and conditional independencies. It develops directed Bayesian networks, including discrete, polynomial-regression, generative, latent-variable, and linear-Gaussian models; explains conditional independence, d-separation, explaining away, and Markov blankets; and develops undirected Markov random fields, clique and energy factorization, moralization, and image-denoising optimization. It presents exact inference through sum-product, max-sum, junction trees, and treewidth, approximate loopy belief propagation, and Bayesian structure learning, while addressing computational limitations. Exercises reinforce normalization, factorization, independence, d-separation, noisy-OR and relevance-vector models, Gaussian recursions, graph enumeration, ICM, MAP inference, and message passing on chains, trees, factor graphs, and cyclic graphs.

nodes.title: 9 Mixture Models and EM
9.1. K -means Clustering
9.1.1 Image segmentation and compression
nodes.summary: The text extends K-means to K-medoids using general dissimilarities, describing its hard-assignment E step, prototype-search M step, and computational costs, then motivates probabilistic soft assignments for ambiguous points. It illustrates K-means through RGB image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression, including the encoding formula, numerical image example, compression ratios, quality trade-off, and the potential benefit of clustering pixel blocks. Finally, it introduces Gaussian mixtures as weighted Gaussian sums represented with a 1-of-K latent variable, whose states are governed by mixing coefficients and whose joint distribution is built from latent and conditional distributions.

This section introduces K-means clustering as an alternating optimization method that assigns data points to their nearest prototypes and recomputes prototypes as cluster means, minimizing a squared-distance distortion measure while converging potentially to a local minimum. It illustrates the algorithm on the Old Faithful data, extends the ideas to K-medoids and general dissimilarities, and motivates soft probabilistic assignments. Applications to RGB image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression are discussed, including encoding, compression-quality trade-offs, and block clustering. The section concludes by introducing Gaussian mixture models and their 1-of-K latent-variable representation as a probabilistic foundation for subsequent EM treatment.

nodes.title: 9.2. Mixtures of Gaussians
9.2.1 Maximum likelihood
nodes.summary: The text explains posterior component responsibilities in Gaussian mixture models, their Bayesian interpretation, and how to sample and visualize complete, incomplete, and responsibility-labeled data. It formulates the mixture-model likelihood for i.i.d. data and discusses the major problems of maximum likelihood, including covariance-collapse singularities, overfitting, heuristic remedies, and label-switching non-identifiability. Because the likelihood lacks a closed-form maximizer, it motivates EM as a broadly applicable alternative, then begins its Gaussian-mixture derivation by obtaining responsibility-weighted updates for component means and defining each component’s effective sample size.

nodes.title: 9.2.2 EM for Gaussian mixtures
EM for Gaussian Mixtures
nodes.summary: The text explains EM for Gaussian mixtures through an illustration and a formal algorithm. Responsibilities softly assign points to components, while the M step updates each component’s mean, covariance, and mixing coefficient using those assignments; repeated cycles gradually approach convergence but are slower and more expensive than K-means. K-means is therefore often used for initialization. Practical issues include avoiding likelihood singularities and recognizing that EM may converge to a local rather than global maximum. The complete procedure specifies initialization, E- and M-step formulas, likelihood evaluation, and a convergence test. The text then introduces an alternative latent-variable perspective, expressing the observed-data likelihood as a log of a sum or integral over latent variables and emphasizing the difficulty caused by this operation occurring inside the logarithm.

EM estimates Gaussian-mixture parameters by alternating responsibility computation in the E step with responsibility-weighted parameter updates in the M step. The resulting mean, covariance, and mixing-coefficient formulas, effective component counts, likelihood-improvement and convergence properties, initialization and practical limitations, and an Old Faithful illustration are presented. The section also motivates EM more generally through latent-variable likelihoods, where sums or integrals inside logarithms make direct maximization difficult.

This section develops Gaussian mixtures as latent-variable models, showing how a 1-of-K component indicator produces the usual mixture density and enables interpretation through posterior responsibilities, sampling, and data visualization. It formulates maximum-likelihood estimation, explains its singularity, overfitting, and identifiability problems, and motivates EM. EM is then derived for Gaussian mixtures, with responsibility-based E-step calculations and weighted mean, covariance, and mixing-coefficient updates in the M step, followed by discussion of effective sample sizes, likelihood and convergence behavior, initialization and practical issues, an Old Faithful example, and the general difficulty of optimizing latent-variable likelihoods.

nodes.title: 9.3. An Alternative View of EM
The General EM Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces EM as a method for maximizing likelihoods with latent or missing variables. It contrasts incomplete observed data with hypothetical complete data, defines the E-step posterior and expected complete-data log likelihood Q, and describes the M-step optimization and iterative convergence procedure. It also extends EM to MAP estimation through a parameter prior, explains its use for missing-at-random data, and begins applying the latent-variable formulation to Gaussian mixture models, where observed component labels would remove the logarithm-over-sum difficulty.

nodes.title: 9.3.1 Gaussian mixtures revisited
nodes.summary: The text presents EM as an iterative latent-variable method that alternates posterior inference for hidden variables with maximization of their expected complete-data log likelihood, including a MAP extension through a parameter prior. It explains EM's application to missing data under a missing-at-random condition. For Gaussian mixtures, it contrasts the difficult incomplete-data likelihood with the simple complete-data likelihood, derives the role of component assignments and mixing proportions, shows that posterior expected assignments are responsibilities, and recovers the standard closed-form EM updates. It concludes by relating soft-assignment Gaussian-mixture EM to hard-assignment K-means, which arises as a limiting case with shared isotropic covariances.

nodes.title: 9.3.2 Relation to K -means
nodes.summary: The section derives EM for Gaussian mixtures by showing that the latent-variable posterior factorizes, identifying its expectations as component responsibilities, and expressing the expected complete-data log likelihood in terms of those responsibilities. Alternating responsibility evaluation and parameter maximization gives the standard EM updates. It then shows that K-means is the zero-variance limit of EM with isotropic shared covariances: soft assignments become hard nearest-mean assignments, the mean and mixing-weight updates reduce to K-means behavior, and likelihood maximization becomes distortion minimization. The section concludes by introducing Bernoulli mixture models, or latent class analysis, as a discrete-variable application of EM and a basis for hidden Markov models.

nodes.title: 9.3.3 Mixtures of Bernoulli distributions
nodes.summary: The text first shows that EM for an isotropic Gaussian mixture with vanishing fixed variance becomes K-means: responsibilities become hard nearest-mean assignments, mean updates match K-means, mixing coefficients reflect cluster fractions, and the expected complete-data likelihood reduces to the K-means distortion objective. It then develops mixtures of Bernoulli distributions for binary data, deriving their moments, latent-variable formulation, likelihood, EM responsibilities, weighted parameter updates, and mixing-coefficient updates, while discussing bounded likelihoods, digit-image clustering, beta and Dirichlet priors, and multinomial extensions. Finally, it begins an EM treatment of Bayesian linear-regression evidence by treating the weights as latent variables, computing their posterior in the E step, and optimizing the hyperparameters α and β using the expected complete-data log likelihood.

nodes.title: 9.3.4 EM for Bayesian linear regression
nodes.summary: The text discusses Bernoulli mixtures for binarized digit images, including priors, EM inference, multinomial extensions, and Dirichlet priors. It then applies EM to Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector machines, deriving hyperparameter re-estimation equations and showing their equivalence to evidence-based updates. Finally, it presents the general EM framework for latent-variable maximum likelihood, introducing the observed/hidden-variable notation, the likelihood marginalization, and its decomposition into an expected complete-data log likelihood plus a KL divergence, which motivates EM and variational inference.

This section presents EM both as the standard iterative algorithm and as an alternative latent-variable perspective. It covers posterior inference and expected complete-data maximization, convergence, MAP and missing-data extensions, and the likelihood/KL decomposition underlying EM. Applications include Gaussian mixtures and their relation to K-means, Bernoulli and multinomial mixture models for binary or categorical data, and Bayesian linear regression with evidence-based hyperparameter re-estimation.

nodes.title: 9.4. The EM Algorithm in General
nodes.summary: The text completes mixture-model re-estimation formulas and develops a general proof and interpretation of EM using a likelihood decomposition into a variational lower bound and KL divergence. It explains the E and M steps, their monotonic likelihood improvement, the expected complete-data objective, graphical and factorized-data interpretations, MAP-EM, GEM and ECM extensions, partial optimization, and incremental EM with sufficient-statistic updates. It concludes with exercises on finite K-means convergence and deriving stochastic K-means via Robbins-Monro.

nodes.title: 9.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text describes incremental EM for independent latent-variable data: responsibilities and exponential-family sufficient statistics are updated one data point at a time, with Gaussian-mixture formulas for updating component means and effective counts. The method has constant per-step cost, may converge faster than batch EM, and preserves the monotonic-improvement and likelihood-maximization properties of EM. It then presents exercises on finite convergence of K-means and deriving stochastic K-means through Robbins-Monro estimation.

nodes.title: 9.3 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Gaussian mixture models and EM: deriving the Gaussian-mixture marginal, extending EM from maximum likelihood to MAP estimation, proving posterior factorization of latent variables across observations using d-separation, deriving EM updates under a shared covariance constraint, interpreting complete-data maximum likelihood estimates, verifying closed-form responsibility-weighted updates for component means, covariances, and mixing coefficients, and deriving the conditional mixture form when the observed vector is partitioned into two parts.

nodes.title: 9.7 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Gaussian mixture models and EM: deriving the Gaussian-mixture marginal from latent-variable distributions; extending EM from maximum likelihood to MAP estimation; proving posterior factorization of latent assignments across observations using d-separation; deriving EM updates under a shared covariance constraint; verifying complete-data maximum-likelihood estimates for component parameters and mixing weights; deriving closed-form responsibility-weighted updates for means, covariances, and mixing coefficients; and showing that conditioning a partitioned mixture distribution produces another mixture with updated weights and conditional component densities.

nodes.title: 9.8 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Gaussian mixture models and EM. It covers deriving the Gaussian-mixture marginal from latent-variable and conditional distributions; extending EM from maximum likelihood to MAP estimation; proving posterior factorization of mixture-model latent variables across observations using d-separation; deriving EM updates under a shared covariance constraint; interpreting complete-data likelihood maximization as independent component fitting with group-based mixing proportions; verifying closed-form updates for component means, covariances, and mixing coefficients; and deriving the conditional mixture form, weights, and component densities after partitioning the observed vector.

nodes.title: 9.10 ( ) Consider a density model given by a mixture distribution
nodes.summary: Exercises 9.3–9.17 develop Gaussian and Bernoulli mixture-model theory and EM updates. They establish Gaussian-mixture marginalization, MAP-EM modifications, posterior factorization, shared-covariance EM, complete-data and expected-likelihood parameter updates, the conditional-mixture property, and the connection between small-variance EM and K-means. They also derive general mixture moments, analyze a degenerate one-step-convergent Bernoulli-mixture initialization, recover Bernoulli mixtures by marginalization, derive Bernoulli mean and mixing-coefficient M steps, and prove that Bernoulli-mixture likelihoods are bounded and free of infinite singularities.

nodes.title: 9.12 ( ) www Consider a mixture distribution of the form
nodes.summary: Exercises 9.11–9.17 examine Gaussian mixtures, general mixture moments, and Bernoulli-mixture EM. They ask for the limiting connection between EM and K-means, derivation of mixture means and covariances, analysis of a degenerate equal-component EM solution, recovery of the Bernoulli mixture by marginalizing latent variables, derivation of the M-step updates for component means and mixing coefficients, and proof that Bernoulli-mixture likelihoods are bounded and therefore free of infinite-likelihood singularities.

nodes.title: 9.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 9.11–9.17 examine Gaussian-mixture EM and K-means equivalence, mean and covariance formulas for general mixtures, degeneracy and convergence properties of Bernoulli-mixture EM, marginalization of latent variables, derivation of Bernoulli-mixture M-step updates for means and mixing coefficients, and boundedness of the Bernoulli-mixture likelihood preventing infinite-likelihood singularities.

nodes.title: 9.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The exercises cover theoretical and derivational aspects of mixture models and EM. They connect Gaussian-mixture EM to K-means, derive moments of general mixtures, analyze degeneracy and convergence in Bernoulli mixtures, derive Bernoulli and multinomial-mixture EM updates, establish likelihood boundedness, and extend EM with beta and Dirichlet priors. They also derive EM hyperparameter updates for Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector machines, compare EM with direct evidence maximization, verify variational-bound and KL-divergence identities and gradient properties, and develop incremental EM updates for Gaussian-mixture means, covariances, and mixing coefficients.

This section develops mixture models and the EM algorithm from latent-variable marginalization and clustering foundations. It introduces K-means, K-medoids, image segmentation, and vector quantization, then develops Gaussian mixtures, their latent assignments and responsibilities, maximum-likelihood issues, and complete EM update equations. It presents EM through variational and likelihood/KL perspectives and extends it to MAP, missing-data, generalized, ECM, partial, and incremental forms. Applications include Bernoulli and multinomial mixtures, Bayesian linear regression, and relevance vector machines, with exercises covering convergence, K-means limits, mixture moments and conditional distributions, Gaussian and Bernoulli EM derivations, priors, likelihood boundedness, posterior factorization, variational identities, and online sufficient-statistic updates.

nodes.title: 10 Approximate Inference
10.1. Variational Inference
10.1.1 Factorized distributions
nodes.summary: The text explains variational inference as approximating an intractable posterior with a tractable, preferably flexible family, either through parametric optimization or factorization into independent groups. It derives the mean-field update rule: each optimal factor is proportional to the exponential of the expected log joint distribution over all other factors, and describes iterative coordinate updates and their convergence. It then begins examining the properties and errors of factorized approximations using a correlated two-dimensional Gaussian, while also including a sidebar biography of Leonhard Euler and a figure illustrating Gaussian variational and Laplace approximations.

nodes.title: 10.1.2 Properties of factorized approximations
nodes.summary: The text derives coordinate-wise optimal factors for variational inference, explains their coupled iterative solution and convergence, and analyzes factorized approximations using a correlated Gaussian example, showing correct means but overly concentrated variances. It compares KL(q||p) with KL(p||q), deriving marginal factors for the reverse direction and explaining their contrasting behavior for low-density regions and multimodal distributions, including implications for expectation propagation. It then places both divergences within the alpha-divergence family, discusses support-seeking versus support-covering behavior and the Hellinger case, and introduces a factorized variational treatment of a Gaussian model with unknown mean and precision under conjugate priors.

nodes.title: 10.1.3 Example: The univariate Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text discusses alpha-divergences and their KL and Hellinger special cases, emphasizing zero-forcing versus zero-avoiding behavior when approximating a fixed distribution. It then develops a factorized variational approximation for the posterior of the mean and precision of a univariate Gaussian: the likelihood and conjugate Gaussian-Gamma priors are specified, Gaussian and gamma optimal factors are derived, and their coupled moment updates are solved iteratively. A figure illustrates convergence toward the optimal factorized approximation. Finally, the text introduces an explicit treatment using broad noninformative priors and begins deriving the associated moment equations.

This section introduces variational inference as a deterministic approach to otherwise intractable Bayesian inference. It explains calculus of variations and derives the evidence lower bound/KL-divergence formulation, then develops mean-field factorized approximations with coordinate-update algorithms and convergence behavior. Through correlated Gaussian examples, it examines approximation errors, variance concentration, forward versus reverse KL divergence, alpha-divergences, and support-seeking versus support-covering behavior. It applies these ideas to estimating the mean and precision of a univariate Gaussian under conjugate and noninformative priors, deriving Gaussian and gamma factors, iterative moment equations, and convergence illustrations, with supplementary historical and graphical material.

This section introduces approximate inference as a response to the difficulty of computing latent-variable posteriors and their expectations exactly in complex or high-dimensional probabilistic models. It develops variational inference through variational calculus, lower bounds, KL divergences, and mean-field coordinate updates, analyzes approximation behavior using correlated Gaussian examples and different divergence measures, and applies the resulting methods to Bayesian estimation of a Gaussian mean and precision, including factor derivations, iterative equations, convergence, and supplementary historical and graphical discussions.

Appendix C compiles material spanning probabilistic foundations and machine-learning methods. It develops Gaussian, Student’s t, periodic, mixture, exponential-family, beta, binomial, Dirichlet, gamma, Wishart, and related distributions; derives conditional, marginal, Bayesian, maximum-likelihood, sequential, and conjugate Bayesian inference; and covers entropy, KL divergence, normalization, moments, matrix geometry, and nonparametric density estimation. It then presents linear regression and classification, neural networks, kernel methods, Gaussian processes, sparse kernel machines, graphical models, mixture models and EM, and variational approximate inference, including their mathematical derivations, computational methods, uncertainty treatments, model selection, regularization, and applications. The appendix also contains broad exercises on probability, linear algebra, estimation, optimization, Bayesian modeling, kernels, neural networks, graphical inference, EM, and variational methods.

nodes.title: Appendix B
10.1.4 Model comparison
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational estimate of Gaussian precision, showing that it produces the unbiased sample variance, then develops variational model comparison using the factorization q(Z,m)=q(Z|m)q(m), a model-specific evidence lower bound, and the update q(m) proportional to p(m) exp(Lₘ), enabling model selection or averaging. It then introduces variational inference for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, specifying latent component assignments, the assignment and data likelihoods, the use of precision matrices, and a symmetric Dirichlet conjugate prior over mixing coefficients.

nodes.title: 10.2. Illustration: Variational Mixture of Gaussians
10.2.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian inference for a conjugate mixture of K Gaussians. It specifies the graphical model, Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart priors, complete joint distribution, and a minimal variational factorization. Coordinate optimization yields categorical assignment distributions characterized by normalized responsibilities, Dirichlet posteriors for mixing proportions, and Gaussian-Wishart posteriors for component means and precisions, with updates based on responsibility-weighted sufficient statistics. Required expectations produce responsibilities analogous to EM, leading to iterative variational E- and M-steps. The discussion explains component pruning and the influence of α0, illustrates results on Old Faithful data, and compares the Bayesian method with maximum-likelihood EM in computation, robustness, overfitting, and model-size selection. It then introduces the variational lower bound, its decomposition into expected likelihood, priors, and entropy terms, its monotonicity as a convergence check, and initial formulas for evaluating its terms.

nodes.title: 10.2.2 Variational lower bound
nodes.summary: This passage explains the benefits of priors and variational inference for Gaussian mixtures, then develops the variational lower bound, its component terms, and its uses for convergence monitoring, implementation checks, and deriving update equations. It concludes with the integral expression for the Bayesian predictive density of a new observation.

nodes.title: 10.2.3 Predictive density
nodes.summary: The text completes the variational lower-bound expressions for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture, explaining their entropy and normalization terms and showing how maximizing the bound recovers the conjugate variational re-estimation equations. It then derives the variational predictive density for a new observation as a mixture of Student's t-distributions, specifying the component means, precisions, degrees of freedom, and weights, with a Gaussian-mixture limit for large data sets. Finally, it introduces selecting the number of components via the lower bound and discusses the K! label-switching symmetry of mixture parameters, which is immaterial for maximum likelihood but must be accounted for in Bayesian marginalization.

nodes.title: 10.2.4 Determining the number of components
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational predictive distribution for a Gaussian mixture as a mixture of Student’s t-distributions that approaches a Gaussian mixture with abundant data. It then discusses selecting the number of components, addressing label-switching multimodality with an ln K! correction, contrasting Bayesian model comparison with maximum likelihood, and presenting an alternative point-estimation approach that automatically prunes irrelevant components. Finally, it explains induced factorizations in variational posteriors, their computational importance, and a d-separation-based criterion for identifying when further factorization is valid.

nodes.title: 10.2.5 Induced factorizations
nodes.summary: The text explains automatic relevance determination in variational Gaussian mixtures, where irrelevant components are pruned, and develops the concept of induced posterior factorizations arising from assumed variational structure and graphical-model conditional independences. It gives the conditional-independence and d-separation criterion for detecting such factorizations and applies it to mixture-model parameters. It then introduces variational Bayesian linear regression, contrasting it with evidence-based point estimation, fixing the noise precision, specifying the Gaussian likelihood and weight prior, placing a conjugate gamma prior on the weight precision, defining the joint model, and motivating approximation of the posterior over weights and precision.

This section illustrates variational Bayesian inference through conjugate Gaussian mixtures, deriving the model, priors, variational factorization, responsibility and parameter updates, lower-bound evaluation, convergence checks, and Student's t predictive distribution. It explains component pruning, prior effects, model-size selection, label-switching, and comparisons with maximum-likelihood EM, then discusses induced factorizations using graphical-model independence and extends the ideas to variational Bayesian linear regression.

nodes.title: 10.3. Variational Linear Regression
10.3.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text explains d-separation-based validation of variational factorizations, then develops mean-field variational inference for Bayesian linear regression with known noise precision and a gamma prior on the weight precision. It derives gamma and Gaussian updates for the precision and weights, their moments, the alternating optimization procedure, and the equivalence to evidence-based estimation under a broad hyperprior. It concludes with the Gaussian predictive distribution for a new input, accounting for observation noise and posterior parameter uncertainty.

nodes.title: 10.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the Gaussian variational posterior for linear-regression weights and the Gamma posterior moments for the precision α, explains alternating variational updates and their equivalence to evidence-based EM under an improper broad α prior, and obtains the Gaussian predictive distribution with input-dependent variance. It then defines and evaluates the variational lower bound through expected likelihood, prior, and entropy terms, and shows that this bound supports selecting the correct polynomial degree while avoiding the overfitting favored by maximum likelihood.

nodes.title: 10.3.3 Lower bound
nodes.summary: The text completes variational linear regression by giving its predictive variance and the explicit variational lower-bound components, then explains how the bound supports Bayesian polynomial-order selection and avoids the overfitting of maximum likelihood. It describes a synthetic-data example where the bound correctly selects a cubic model. It then introduces exponential-family distributions, distinguishes latent variables from fixed-dimensional parameters, gives Gaussian-mixture examples, states the IID exponential-family joint form and its conjugate prior, and interprets the prior hyperparameters as pseudo-observations before beginning a variational analysis.

This section develops variational linear regression by deriving mean-field posterior updates for weights and precision, their moments and alternating optimization, and their connection to evidence-based estimation. It obtains the noise- and uncertainty-aware Gaussian predictive distribution, formulates the variational lower bound, and demonstrates its use for Bayesian polynomial-order selection without maximum-likelihood overfitting. It concludes by introducing exponential-family models, latent-variable distinctions, conjugate priors, and the pseudo-observation interpretation of prior hyperparameters.

nodes.title: 10.4. Exponential Family Distributions
nodes.summary: The text illustrates model-order selection through a lower-bound plot, then develops variational inference for exponential-family complete-data models with conjugate priors. It distinguishes latent variables from parameters, derives factorized variational posteriors and their sufficient-statistic updates, and describes the coupled iterative variational E and M steps. It then generalizes variational inference to directed graphical models, showing that factor updates depend locally on each node's Markov blanket and can be implemented through conjugate-exponential message passing, enabling efficient, scalable inference and lower-bound evaluation in large networks.

nodes.title: 10.5. Local Variational Methods
nodes.summary: The text introduces local variational inference as a factorwise alternative to global posterior approximation and develops it through convex duality. Tangent lines provide lower bounds for convex functions and conjugate-function representations, with corresponding minimum-based upper bounds for concave functions. The exponential example illustrates the derivation and optimization of a variational linear bound. Transformations enable the method to handle nonconvex functions: applying conjugacy to the log logistic sigmoid gives an entropy-based exponential upper bound, while the Jaakkola-Jordan transformation yields a Gaussian-form lower bound parameterized by ξ. This bound makes sigmoid-Gaussian integrals tractable, though optimizing ξ produces a generally inexact compromise. The text then begins variational Bayesian logistic regression, explaining that the local quadratic bound leads to a Gaussian posterior and a rigorous evidence lower bound, and rewrites the binary logistic likelihood in a form suitable for applying the bound.

nodes.title: 10.6. Variational Logistic Regression
10.6.1 Variational posterior distribution
nodes.summary: This section develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using the Jaakkola–Jordan local quadratic lower bound on the logistic sigmoid. Each observation receives a variational parameter, producing a quadratic approximation to the likelihood and, with a Gaussian prior, a Gaussian variational posterior whose mean and covariance are given explicitly. The method optimizes a rigorous lower bound on the marginal likelihood, offers improved accuracy over Laplace approximation, and supports batch or sequential learning, though the presented sigmoid bound is limited to binary classification. The variational parameters are optimized either by EM or by analytical integration over the weights followed by direct maximization; the text introduces the EM procedure.

nodes.title: 10.6.2 Optimizing the variational parameters
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using a quadratic bound to obtain a Gaussian posterior over the weights, explains its improved flexibility over Laplace inference and applicability to batch or sequential binary classification, and derives optimization of the local variational parameters through either EM or direct analytical maximization. It gives the ξ re-estimation rule, the closed-form marginal-likelihood lower bound, and the sequential predictive procedure, illustrates uncertainty and large-margin behavior, and begins extending the framework to infer the prior hyperparameter α through combined global and local variational approximations.

nodes.title: 10.6.3 Inference of hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text illustrates variational Bayesian logistic regression, including its predictive uncertainty, posterior-sampled decision boundaries, sequential-update interpretation, and connection to large-margin behavior. It then develops joint variational inference for logistic-regression weights and an unknown Gaussian-prior precision α using a gamma hyperprior, deriving Gaussian and gamma variational factors, local-parameter updates, required moments, and an iterative optimization scheme. Finally, it introduces expectation propagation, explaining that reverse-KL minimization within the exponential family leads to matching expected sufficient statistics between the approximation and target distributions.

The section develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using the Jaakkola–Jordan sigmoid bound, yielding a Gaussian weight posterior and a tractable marginal-likelihood lower bound. It covers EM and direct optimization of local variational parameters, batch and sequential prediction, uncertainty and large-margin interpretations, and the method’s limitation to binary classification. It then extends inference to an unknown prior precision through gamma–Gaussian variational factors and concludes with expectation propagation as an alternative based on exponential-family moment matching.

nodes.title: 10.7. Expectation Propagation
Expectation Propagation
nodes.summary: The text derives the EP factor-update normalization and presents the complete expectation propagation algorithm for approximating posterior distributions and model evidence through iterative factor removal, moment matching, and reinsertion. It compares EP with assumed density filtering and variational Bayes, discussing data-order effects, convergence guarantees, energy functions, KL-divergence directions, and strengths or weaknesses for multimodal, mixture, and logistic models. It then introduces a Gaussian clutter example: observations arise from a mixture of a signal Gaussian centered at θ and background Gaussian clutter, with a Gaussian prior on θ. Exact inference produces 2^N mixture components and is exponentially expensive, so EP approximates the posterior using prior and likelihood factors and a spherical Gaussian q(θ).

nodes.title: 10.7.1 Example: The clutter problem
nodes.summary: The text presents EP using a Gaussian-mixture clutter problem in which the mean of a target Gaussian must be inferred from observations contaminated by known Gaussian background clutter. Because the exact posterior contains 2^N Gaussian components, EP approximates it with a spherical Gaussian and replaces each likelihood factor with an exponential-quadratic approximation. It describes initialization, cavity formation, tilted-distribution moments, factor refinement, iteration and convergence, evidence evaluation, and the interpretation of potentially negative factor variance parameters. Figures illustrate the clutter problem, factor approximations, and comparisons with variational Bayes and Laplace methods. The section then introduces EP for graphical models, where factors depend on subsets of variables and are represented using factor graphs.

nodes.title: 10.7.2 Expectation propagation on graphs
nodes.summary: This text concludes the clutter-problem discussion of EP by describing convergence, evidence estimation, unusual factor variances, illustrative approximations, and performance comparisons with variational Bayes and Laplace methods. It then develops EP on factor graphs, showing through a concrete example and a general derivation that fully factorized EP updates are equivalent to sum-product belief propagation, with sequential updates recovering the standard algorithm and exact inference on trees. It discusses more flexible grouped or partially disconnected approximations, the open problem of selecting them, and the unifying role of alpha-divergence message-passing methods. The included exercises cover KL decompositions, moment matching, mean-field optimization, and Gaussian KL minimization.

The section finishes the variational Bayes re-estimation scheme and then develops expectation propagation as reverse-KL, moment-matching approximate inference. EP approximates posterior factors with exponential-family terms, updates them iteratively through cavity and tilted distributions, and provides evidence estimates. Its properties and relationship to variational methods, assumed density filtering, convergence, and divergence choices are examined, followed by a detailed Gaussian clutter example and comparisons with other approximations. The method is then generalized to factor graphs, where it connects to belief propagation and exact tree inference, with discussion of structured approximations, alpha-divergences, and related exercises.

nodes.title: 11 Sampling Methods
11.1. Basic Sampling Algorithms
11.1.1 Standard distributions
nodes.summary: The text introduces basic sampling methods, beginning with pseudo-random uniform number generation and the inverse-transformation method for obtaining samples from nonuniform distributions. It illustrates this with exponential and Cauchy distributions, explains the multivariate Jacobian formulation, and presents the Box–Muller method for generating standard Gaussian variables. It then shows how to form shifted, scaled, and multivariate Gaussian samples using Cholesky decomposition. Because inverse transformation is limited to distributions with tractable invertible integrals, the text motivates rejection and importance sampling, beginning rejection sampling for unnormalized target densities and easily sampled proposal distributions.

nodes.title: 11.1.2 Rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text completes the Gaussian transformation method, showing how independent standard normals and the Cholesky decomposition generate univariate and multivariate Gaussian variables. Because transformation sampling is limited by the need to invert integrals, it introduces rejection sampling: an unnormalized target is enclosed by a scaled, easily sampled proposal, and proposal points are accepted according to an envelope test, with efficiency determined by the envelope area. A generalized Cauchy envelope is applied to gamma sampling, and adaptive rejection sampling is then introduced, using tangent-line envelopes for log-concave densities and refining them with rejected samples.

nodes.title: 11.1.3 Adaptive rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text discusses optimized rejection sampling for a gamma distribution using a scaled Cauchy proposal, then introduces adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave targets. It explains how tangent lines form a piecewise-exponential envelope, how rejected samples refine it, derivative-free and Metropolis-Hastings extensions, and the severe exponential inefficiency of rejection sampling in high dimensions. It then introduces importance sampling as a way to estimate expectations by sampling from an easy proposal distribution and weighting samples by the target-to-proposal density ratio, avoiding inefficient high-dimensional uniform grids.

nodes.title: 11.1.4 Importance sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains importance sampling as a way to estimate expectations under a difficult distribution by sampling from an easier proposal and applying density-ratio weights. It derives both ordinary and self-normalized estimators for distributions known with or without normalization constants, contrasts the method with inefficient uniform-grid evaluation, and emphasizes proposal quality, effective sample size, weight degeneracy, uncovered important regions, and the possibility of undetected large errors. It then describes uniform and likelihood-weighted sampling for discrete graphical models, including their weighting rules and limitations, introduces adaptive self-importance sampling, and transitions to sampling-importance-resampling while noting the difficulty of selecting rejection-sampling constants.

nodes.title: 11.1.5 Sampling-importance-resampling
nodes.summary: The text explains limitations and failure modes of importance sampling, especially weight degeneracy and missed high-probability regions, and emphasizes choosing a sampling distribution that covers the target. It describes uniform sampling, likelihood-weighted ancestral sampling, and self-importance sampling for graphical models. It then presents sampling-importance-resampling, including its weighted resampling procedure, asymptotic justification, finite-sample behavior, special case q=p, and direct moment estimation. Finally, it explains Monte Carlo EM, its MAP extension, and stochastic EM for mixture models.

nodes.title: 11.1.6 Sampling and the EM algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how weighted sampling estimates expectations and how Monte Carlo methods approximate the EM algorithm’s E-step, yielding Monte Carlo EM, its MAP extension, and stochastic EM for mixture models. It then introduces Bayesian data augmentation, which alternates imputation and posterior-sampling steps to approximate parameter and latent-variable posteriors. Finally, it motivates Markov chain Monte Carlo by noting the high-dimensional limitations of rejection and importance sampling.

This section develops basic methods for sampling and Monte Carlo inference. It begins with uniform generation, inverse transformation, Gaussian construction, and Cholesky-based multivariate sampling; then presents rejection and adaptive rejection sampling, including proposal envelopes, efficiency, log-concavity, and high-dimensional limitations. It introduces importance sampling and its normalized variants, analyzes proposal quality and weight degeneracy, and covers graphical-model sampling, adaptive methods, and sampling-importance-resampling. Finally, it applies weighted sampling to Monte Carlo, MAP, and stochastic EM, introduces Bayesian data augmentation, and motivates Markov chain Monte Carlo.

nodes.title: 11.2. Markov Chain Monte Carlo
11.2.1 Markov chains
nodes.summary: The text motivates Markov chain Monte Carlo by showing that ordinary random walks explore state spaces inefficiently, with displacement growing only as the square root of time, and illustrates Metropolis sampling of a Gaussian. It then defines first-order and homogeneous Markov chains, explains transition-based marginal propagation, invariant distributions, detailed balance and reversibility, and the ergodicity required for convergence to a unique equilibrium target distribution. It describes forming composite transitions by mixtures or successive base transitions and the conditions under which invariance and detailed balance are preserved. Finally, it introduces Metropolis-Hastings for asymmetric proposals, gives its acceptance probability and detailed-balance proof, notes that normalization is unnecessary and symmetric proposals recover Metropolis, and begins discussing how proposal variance affects efficiency.

nodes.title: 11.2.2 The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how Markov transitions can be mixed or composed, when invariance and detailed balance are preserved, and how symmetric ordering can restore detailed balance for compositions. It then presents Metropolis-Hastings for nonsymmetric proposals, gives its acceptance probability and detailed-balance proof, and discusses how proposal scale affects acceptance, random-walk behavior, and convergence for anisotropic distributions. Finally, it introduces Gibbs sampling as a Metropolis-Hastings special case that updates variables from their full conditional distributions.

This section moves from Bayesian data augmentation to Markov chain Monte Carlo as a general method for sampling difficult posterior distributions. It explains the Metropolis random-walk algorithm, Markov-chain dynamics, stationary and invariant distributions, detailed balance, reversibility, ergodicity, and the correlation of generated samples. It then covers combining transition kernels, generalizes Metropolis to asymmetric proposals through Metropolis-Hastings, analyzes proposal-scale effects on sampling efficiency, and presents Gibbs sampling as a conditional-update special case.

nodes.title: 11.3. Gibbs Sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains how mismatched scales and correlations make isotropic Metropolis-Hastings sampling inefficient, producing high rejection rates or slow random walks whose mixing time grows with the ratio of distributional length scales. It then develops Gibbs sampling as conditional, coordinate-wise MCMC and as an always-accepted special case of Metropolis-Hastings, covering its algorithm, invariance, ergodicity, initialization, and autocorrelation. Its behavior on correlated Gaussians motivates over-relaxation, including the Gaussian update formula and ordered generalization. The discussion addresses implementation through graphical-model Markov blankets, conjugacy, log-concavity, adaptive rejection sampling, ICM as a greedy alternative, and blocking Gibbs sampling. Finally, it introduces slice sampling as an automatically adaptive augmented-variable method based on uniform sampling under an unnormalized density, alongside illustrative figures and a biography of Josiah Willard Gibbs.

nodes.title: 11.4. Slice Sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains Gibbs sampling and its graphical-model Markov blankets, practical sampling of full conditionals, ICM as a greedy Gibbs approximation, and blocking to reduce sample dependence. It then presents slice sampling, including its auxiliary-variable formulation, uniform-under-the-density interpretation, adaptive interval expansion and shrinking procedure, and multivariate extension. Finally, it introduces hybrid Monte Carlo as a gradient-based method for continuous distributions that avoids Metropolis random walks, beginning its formulation through Hamiltonian dynamics with position and momentum variables.

nodes.title: 11.5. The Hybrid Monte Carlo Algorithm
11.5.1 Dynamical systems
nodes.summary: The text finishes the discussion of multivariate slice sampling, then introduces hybrid Monte Carlo as a gradient-based method for avoiding Metropolis random walks in continuous state spaces. It develops Hamiltonian dynamics from position variables and momenta, defines potential, kinetic, and total Hamiltonian energy, and derives Hamilton's equations. It explains conservation of energy and phase-space volume through Liouville's theorem, showing that the joint distribution proportional to exp(-H) is invariant. Because fixed energy is not ergodic, momentum variables are periodically resampled from their Gaussian conditional distribution. Practical numerical integration is performed with the volume-preserving leapfrog scheme, whose residual discretization errors are corrected by the later Metropolis step. The section concludes by emphasizing the efficiency of gradient information in high-dimensional sampling and includes a biographical sidebar on William Rowan Hamilton.

nodes.title: 11.5.2 Hybrid Monte Carlo
nodes.summary: The text explains Hybrid Monte Carlo as Metropolis-corrected leapfrog Hamiltonian dynamics, including its acceptance rule, time-reversal and volume-preservation properties, detailed-balance proof, and an ergodicity fix based on randomizing the step size. It analyzes performance on Gaussian targets, showing that the required trajectory length scales linearly with the ratio of largest to smallest standard deviations, compared with quadratic random-walk scaling for simple Metropolis sampling. It then introduces partition functions as normalization constants and Bayesian model evidences, and presents importance sampling as a method for estimating their ratios when direct evaluation is infeasible.

This section develops hybrid Monte Carlo from Hamiltonian dynamics, explaining its energy-based formulation, invariant phase-space distribution, momentum refreshment, leapfrog integration, and Metropolis correction. It covers HMC's reversibility, volume preservation, detailed balance, and randomized step sizes, compares its favorable scaling on Gaussian targets with random-walk Metropolis methods, and concludes with partition functions, Bayesian evidence, and importance-sampling estimates of their ratios, alongside a biographical note on William Rowan Hamilton.

nodes.title: 11.6. Estimating the Partition Function
nodes.summary: The text compares the efficiency of leapfrog HMC and random-walk Metropolis sampling, then explains partition functions, their role in Bayesian model comparison, importance-sampling estimators for partition-function ratios, limitations caused by distribution mismatch, Markov-chain-based importance distributions, and chaining through interpolating intermediate energy functions. It also lists ten exercises covering estimator moments, inverse-transform and Gaussian sampling, Cauchy transformations, change-of-variables proofs, rejection sampling, adaptive rejection sampling, piecewise exponential sampling, and the second moment of a simple random walk.
