This section surveys Monte Carlo methods for approximate inference, beginning with unbiased expectation estimation and graphical-model sampling, then developing rejection and importance sampling and their applications to Monte Carlo, MAP, EM, and data augmentation. It introduces and analyzes MCMC through Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling, including convergence, balance, autocorrelation, blocking, over-relaxation, and practical conditional sampling, followed by slice sampling and gradient-based hybrid Monte Carlo. It concludes with partition-function and Bayesian-evidence estimation, extensive exercises covering the principal algorithms and theoretical properties, and an introduction to continuous latent-variable models and PCA.

Appendix B completes and extends the chapter's treatment of approximate Bayesian inference: it finishes explicit variational updates for a Gaussian example, develops variational model comparison, Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, linear regression, exponential-family and graphical-model inference, local variational bounds, logistic regression, and expectation propagation, including message passing, structured approximations, alpha divergences, and extensive derivational exercises. The appendix also covers verification of mixture, regression, logistic, ADF, and EP results, asymptotic and symmetry properties, and then surveys Monte Carlo, rejection and importance sampling, MCMC, slice and hybrid Monte Carlo, evidence estimation, and continuous latent-variable models including PCA.

nodes.title: Appendix C
12.1.2 Minimum-error formulation
nodes.summary: The text explains PCA as the selection of covariance-matrix eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues to maximize projected variance, including the computation of the mean and covariance, full and partial eigendecomposition costs, and efficient alternatives. It then derives PCA through minimum squared reconstruction error: data are expanded in an orthonormal basis, approximated in an M-dimensional subspace, and optimized over coordinates, offsets, and basis vectors. The optimal approximation is the orthogonal projection through the data mean, with basis directions given by covariance eigenvectors; the minimum distortion equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues, so the largest-eigenvalue directions are retained. It discusses the two-dimensional intuition, the no-reduction case M=D, and the related CCA method for finding correlated subspaces across multiple variables. Finally, it introduces PCA data-compression applications for handwritten digits and lists associated exercises, appendices, figure, and references.

nodes.title: 12.1.3 Applications of peA
nodes.summary: The text derives PCA as covariance-eigenvector optimization: minimizing projection distortion selects the M directions of greatest variance, while distortion equals the sum of discarded eigenvalues. It covers the equal-eigenvalue and no-reduction cases, relates PCA to CCA, and explains applications to digit-image compression, reconstruction, preprocessing, standardization, and whitening. It also contrasts unsupervised PCA with the label-informed Fisher discriminant, presents two-dimensional PCA visualization examples, and introduces computational and rank limitations of PCA when data dimensionality exceeds the number of samples.

nodes.title: 12.1.4 peA for high-dimensional data
nodes.summary: The text compares PCA and Fisher’s linear discriminant, showing that PCA maximizes variance whereas Fisher’s method uses class labels for better separation, and illustrates projection of flow data onto its first two principal components. It then explains an efficient PCA method for high-dimensional data with fewer observations than dimensions: the covariance matrix has many zero eigenvalues, so eigendecomposition can be transferred from the D×D covariance matrix to an N×N matrix, reducing complexity from O(D^3) to O(N^3), with the original eigenvectors recovered by a normalized transformation. Finally, it introduces probabilistic PCA as a maximum-likelihood latent-variable formulation of PCA using a constrained Gaussian model with fewer parameters that can capture dominant data correlations.

nodes.title: 12.2. Probabilistic peA
12.2.1 Maximum likelihood peA
nodes.summary: The text develops maximum-likelihood probabilistic PCA. It derives the optimal mean, characterizes all stationary loading matrices through covariance eigenvectors, identifies the global solution using the leading principal components, and gives the residual-noise variance as the mean discarded eigenvalue. It explains latent-space rotational invariance and non-identifiability, the resulting predictive variances, and the relationship between probabilistic and conventional PCA. Posterior latent projections, their covariance, and the zero-noise limit are described. The section also shows how probabilistic PCA provides a low-parameter compromise between isotropic, diagonal, and full Gaussian covariance models, including its degrees of freedom and limiting cases. Finally, it introduces EM estimation for PPCA, emphasizing its computational benefits in high dimensions, extensibility to factor analysis, and principled treatment of missing data.

nodes.title: 12.2.2 EM algorithm for peA
nodes.summary: The text explains PPCA's parameter efficiency and rotational redundancy, including its limiting cases of full and isotropic covariance. It then derives and describes EM estimation for PPCA, covering the complete-data likelihood, posterior sufficient statistics, W and noise updates, computational advantages over covariance eigendecomposition, online implementation, and principled treatment of missing data. The zero-noise limit recovers an EM form of standard PCA, interpreted through projection and a spring-and-rod analogy. Finally, it introduces Bayesian PCA and practical eigenvalue-spectrum heuristics for selecting the latent dimensionality.

nodes.title: 12.2.3 Bayesian peA
nodes.summary: The text explains EM for probabilistic PCA using a spring-and-rod physical analogy and illustrates its robustness to missing data and iterative subspace updates. It then discusses selecting latent dimensionality through eigenvalue spectra, cross-validation, variational Bayesian model selection, and an ARD-based Bayesian PCA method. Gaussian priors with precision hyperparameters on the columns of W automatically prune irrelevant dimensions; the hyperparameters are optimized using a Laplace-approximated marginal likelihood alongside modified EM updates. The model covers dimensionalities from a full-covariance to an isotropic Gaussian, with computational trade-offs for smaller latent spaces. Gibbs-sampling behavior, comparisons with standard probabilistic PCA, fully Bayesian extensions, and the transition to factor analysis are also presented.

nodes.title: 12.2.4 Factor analysis
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of Bayesian PCA, explaining its Laplace-approximated hyperparameter evidence updates, EM procedure, dimensionality behavior, computational trade-offs, illustrative comparisons, and Gibbs-sampling modes, while noting extensions to fully Bayesian PCA and dimensionality selection. It then introduces factor analysis as a closely related linear-Gaussian latent-variable model with diagonal rather than isotropic observation noise, explaining factor loadings, uniquenesses, covariance structure, rotational non-identifiability, its relationship to PCA, EM estimation, Bayesian treatment, and differing behavior under data transformations. Finally, it begins kernel PCA, presenting it as a nonlinear kernelized version of PCA and setting up the centered-data covariance eigenproblem and feature-space mapping.

This section reformulates PCA as probabilistic PCA, a linear-Gaussian latent-variable model, and develops its maximum-likelihood, EM, and Bayesian treatments. It derives the relationship to conventional PCA, latent posteriors, covariance structure, rotational ambiguity, noise limits, parameter efficiency, computational benefits, missing-data handling, generative and classification uses, and methods for selecting latent dimensionality. It then extends the discussion to Bayesian ARD-based dimensionality pruning and fully Bayesian alternatives, introduces factor analysis with diagonal noise and its estimation and identifiability properties, and begins kernel PCA as a nonlinear feature-space generalization.

nodes.title: 12.3. Kernel peA
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of factor analysis by noting efficient diagonal M-step computations, Bayesian extensions, and its differing transformation behavior relative to PCA and probabilistic PCA. It then introduces kernel PCA as a nonlinear PCA method based on replacing scalar products with kernels. The covariance eigenproblem is reformulated in feature space, showing that eigenvectors and projections can be obtained through an N x N kernel matrix and kernel evaluations alone, with appropriate coefficient normalization and implicit feature-space centering. Kernel PCA can yield up to N nonlinear components, including more than the original data dimension; linear kernels recover standard PCA, while a Gaussian-kernel example demonstrates nonlinear cluster separation. The text also highlights the method's computational cost and the difficulty of reconstructing original-space pre-images from truncated feature-space projections.

nodes.title: 12.4. Nonlinear Latent Variable Models
12.4.1 Independent component analysis
nodes.summary: The text introduces nonlinear and non-Gaussian latent-variable models and focuses on independent component analysis (ICA), in which observed variables are linear mixtures of statistically independent, non-Gaussian latent variables. Using blind source separation as an example, it explains how mixed microphone signals can be unmixed by likelihood-based estimation of the mixing coefficients. It emphasizes that Gaussian latent models cannot identify independent components because rotations leave the likelihood unchanged and only guarantee uncorrelatedness, not independence. Heavy-tailed distributions such as the inverse hyperbolic cosine form are commonly used. The text also discusses information-maximization ICA, probabilistic extensions such as noisy independent factor analysis with Gaussian-mixture latent distributions trained by EM and variational reconstruction, notes the extensive ICA literature, and transitions to autoassociative neural networks.

nodes.title: 12.4.2 Autoassociative neural networks
nodes.summary: The text discusses the need for non-Gaussian latent variables to identify independent components in ICA, explaining the rotational ambiguity of Gaussian latent models and distinguishing uncorrelatedness from independence. It describes heavy-tailed ICA distributions, the information-maximization origin of ICA, and probabilistic extensions such as independent factor analysis. It then examines autoassociative neural networks: two-layer networks, even with nonlinear hidden units, recover ordinary PCA, whereas deeper networks can learn nonlinear dimensionality reductions at the cost of difficult nonconvex optimization and possible local minima. Finally, it surveys nonlinear-manifold modeling through piecewise and probabilistic mixtures of PCA or factor analyzers, Bayesian and hierarchical extensions, and principal curves as nonlinear generalizations of PCA.

nodes.title: 12.4.3 Modelling nonlinear manifolds
nodes.summary: The text surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold models, beginning with nonlinear PCA-like neural networks and their optimization limitations. It covers piecewise-linear mixtures of PCA and factor analysers, principal curves and surfaces, MDS, LLE, and Isomap; discusses latent trait models and exponential-family generalizations; and presents density networks and GTM, including GTM's probabilistic formulation, EM training, relation to SOM, extensions, and geometric diagnostics. It concludes with exercises on PCA eigenvector proofs, probabilistic PCA transformations, graphical structure, marginal and posterior distributions, maximum-likelihood estimation, limiting behavior, and reconstruction.

This section surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold models, beginning with ICA for separating independent non-Gaussian sources and explaining identifiability, heavy-tailed distributions, information maximization, and probabilistic extensions. It then examines autoassociative neural networks for nonlinear dimensionality reduction and their optimization challenges, followed by mixtures of linear latent models, principal curves and surfaces, manifold-learning methods, latent trait and exponential-family models, density networks, and GTM with its probabilistic training and geometric properties. The section concludes with exercises covering theoretical and probabilistic PCA, graphical and distributional analysis, likelihood estimation, limiting cases, and reconstruction.

nodes.summary: This text introduces a set of exercises on probabilistic PCA and related Gaussian transformations. It covers eigenvector normalization and equivalent eigenvector solutions; invariance of the marginal model under general Gaussian latent distributions; affine transformations of Gaussian variables; graphical-model independence structure and its relation to naive Bayes; derivations of the probabilistic PCA marginal and posterior distributions; maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the data mean; and the relationship between probabilistic PCA posterior means, conventional PCA projections, noise-induced shrinkage toward the origin, and optimal least-squares reconstruction.

nodes.title: 12.13 (* *) Show that the optimal reconstruction of a data point under probabilistic PCA, according to the least squares projection cost of conventional PCA, is given by
nodes.summary: This text presents exercises on probabilistic PCA and factor analysis. It covers eigenvector normalization and equivalent parameterizations, Gaussian affine transformations and marginal/posterior derivations, graphical-model independence structure, maximum-likelihood estimation of the mean and its uniqueness, limiting and noisy posterior projections, reconstruction, parameter counting, EM update derivations, and extensions to randomly missing data. It then addresses linear least-squares PCA updates, factor-analysis parameter counting and rotational invariance, mean estimation, and the factor-analysis EM E-step.

nodes.title: 12.19 (**) IIiI!I Show that the factor analysis model described in Section 12.2.4 is invariant under rotations of the latent space coordinates.
nodes.summary: Exercises 12.14–12.29 examine parameter counting and EM derivations for probabilistic PCA and factor analysis, including missing-data PCA, least-squares interpretations of PCA, latent-space rotational invariance, likelihood optimization, and graphical models for PCA mixtures. They also develop an EM algorithm for the multivariate Student's t-distribution, analyze transformation and covariance properties of linear-Gaussian latent-variable models, relate equivalent kernel-PCA eigenvalue formulations and recover linear PCA from the linear kernel, use change-of-variable theory to construct arbitrary densities, and distinguish independence from mere zero correlation through covariance examples.

nodes.title: 13 Sequential Data
13.1. Markov Models
nodes.summary: The text introduces Markov and state space models for sequential data. It contrasts i.i.d. modeling with first- and higher-order Markov chains, explains their factorizations, conditional-independence properties, stationarity, and parameter-growth limitations, and discusses autoregressive and neural-network alternatives. It then introduces latent-state space models, whose latent variables obey a Markov chain while observations can depend on the entire history, and identifies hidden Markov models and linear dynamical systems as key examples. The opening of the HMM section interprets HMMs as temporally coupled mixture models, lists major applications, and defines their discrete latent states and transition-probability matrix.

nodes.title: 13.2. Hidden Markov Models
13.2.1 Maximum likelihood for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains HMMs' ability to model local temporal warping, illustrated with handwritten digits and related to speech-rate variation, while noting their sensitivity to reversed sequence order. It then develops maximum-likelihood learning for HMMs: direct latent-state marginalization is exponentially expensive, so EM is used. The E step computes single-state and consecutive-state posterior probabilities, γ and ξ, and forms the expected complete-data log likelihood; the M step updates initial-state and transition probabilities and fits emission parameters using weighted likelihoods, with specific Gaussian and multinomial formulas and analogous Bernoulli updates. It discusses initialization, preservation of zero transitions, and left-to-right models, and introduces the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm as the efficient exact method for computing the required posteriors.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 The forward-backward algorithm
nodes.summary: The text completes the HMM EM framework by giving emission-specific M-step updates and initialization strategies, then develops the alpha-beta forward-backward algorithm for computing single- and pairwise hidden-state posteriors. It derives the required conditional independences, forward and backward recursions, boundary conditions, computational complexity, likelihood evaluation, and ξ formulas. It explains the full EM training procedure, handling of different emission types and sequence lengths, online predictive distributions, prior-based and variational extensions, and finally shows how the same recursions arise from the sum-product algorithm on a factor-graph representation.

nodes.title: 13.2.3 The sum-product algorithm for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains practical HMM inference and estimation. It notes that forward prediction requires fixed storage, discusses regularized maximum likelihood and fully Bayesian variational extensions, and derives the forward-backward alpha and beta recursions from the sum-product algorithm on a simplified factor graph. It shows how message products yield hidden-state marginals and related pairwise quantities, then introduces scaling because unnormalized forward probabilities rapidly underflow, defining normalized forward probabilities and conditional-data scaling factors to maintain numerical stability.

nodes.title: 13.2.4 Scaling factors
nodes.summary: The text completes the sum-product interpretation of the HMM forward-backward algorithm, showing that alpha and beta messages produce the state and pairwise marginals. It then addresses numerical underflow by introducing normalized alpha and beta variables and scaling factors c_n, derives their forward and backward recursions, and shows that the likelihood is the product of the scaling factors while the required marginals remain recoverable. It also contrasts the standard alpha-beta algorithm with an alternative alpha-gamma recursion. Finally, it introduces the Viterbi algorithm as max-sum message passing for finding the globally most probable hidden-state sequence, explaining why independent marginal maximization is insufficient, why Viterbi is efficient and log-domain stable, and giving its message-passing formulation.

nodes.title: 13.2.5 The Viterbi algorithm
nodes.summary: The text contrasts the alpha-gamma and alpha-beta forward-backward formulations, then introduces the Viterbi algorithm for finding the globally most probable hidden-state sequence rather than independently most probable states. It derives the log-domain max-sum recursion and initialization, explains the dynamic-programming interpretation, linear efficiency, and backtracking procedure, and concludes by discussing HMM extensions, especially discriminative cross-entropy training of class-specific models to improve sequence classification.

nodes.title: 13.2.6 Extensions of the hidden Markov model
nodes.summary: The text explains the dynamic-programming intuition behind Viterbi decoding and surveys important HMM extensions. These include discriminative training for classification, explicit state-duration modeling, autoregressive observations for longer-range dependencies, input-output models for supervised sequences, and factorial models with multiple latent chains. It discusses the conditional independencies, EM or variational inference procedures, computational costs, and limitations of each variant, emphasizing graphical models as a framework for designing and analyzing them. It then introduces linear dynamical systems as models for estimating a changing quantity from noisy sequential measurements, motivating recency-weighted or windowed filtering.

This section introduces hidden Markov models as temporally dependent mixture or state-space models with discrete latent states, specifying their initial distributions, transition matrices, emission distributions, joint probability, graphical and trellis representations, and common emission choices. It develops maximum-likelihood EM learning through state and state-pair posteriors, efficiently computed by the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm and interpretable via sum-product message passing. It covers likelihood evaluation, online prediction, scaling for numerical stability, regularized and Bayesian extensions, and alternative message recursions. It then presents Viterbi max-sum decoding for the most probable complete state sequence and surveys extensions involving discriminative training, state durations, autoregressive and input-output observations, factorial latent chains, and connections to linear dynamical systems.

nodes.title: 13.3. Linear Dynamical Systems
13.3.1 Inference in LDS
nodes.summary: The text develops inference for linear dynamical systems using Gaussian sum-product message passing. It derives the forward Kalman-filter prediction, observation update, Kalman gain, covariance and likelihood normalization, including initial conditions, and explains filtering as prediction followed by correction. It discusses limiting noise regimes and illustrates tracking of a moving object. It then derives the backward Kalman-smoother recursion for posteriors using all observations, explains its dependence on the completed forward pass and its importance for EM parameter learning, and gives the Gaussian pairwise posterior and cross-covariance needed by EM.

nodes.title: 13.3.2 Learning in LDS
nodes.summary: The text derives EM-based maximum-likelihood learning for an LDS, defining the required smoothed posterior moments, expected complete-data log likelihood, and closed-form updates for the initial distribution, transition dynamics, and observation model. It briefly mentions MAP and fully Bayesian extensions, then surveys richer LDS variants: mixture initial states, the impractical exponential growth caused by mixture emissions, approximate inference methods for non-linear or non-Gaussian models including the extended Kalman filter, and switching state-space models that combine continuous LDS chains with discrete switching variables, along with their variational inference treatment and discrete-only switching HMM counterpart.

nodes.title: 13.3.3 Extensions of LDS
nodes.summary: The text reviews maximum-likelihood, MAP, and approximate fully Bayesian parameter learning for linear dynamical systems, then discusses extensions beyond the basic linear-Gaussian model. Gaussian-mixture initial states remain tractable, whereas mixture emissions cause exponentially growing posterior complexity. More general non-Gaussian or nonlinear models require deterministic approximations, sampling, or methods such as the extended Kalman filter. It also presents switching state space models, which combine continuous linear-Gaussian chains with a discrete switching Markov chain; although exact inference is intractable, variational forward-backward methods are effective. A fully discrete counterpart is the switching hidden Markov model.

nodes.title: 13.3.4 Particle filters
nodes.summary: The text develops particle filtering as a sequential Monte Carlo method for non-linear or non-Gaussian dynamical systems. It derives the weighted-sample approximation to the filtering posterior, defines normalized likelihood weights, shows how the predictive distribution becomes a weight-based mixture of transition distributions, and explains the two-stage recursive algorithm of propagating particles and reweighting them using new observations. The required conditional independences are justified by d-separation, alternative names for the method are given, and an exercise asks readers to verify related Markov-model independences.

This section introduces linear dynamical systems as continuous, linear-Gaussian state-space models for tracking changing latent quantities from noisy sequential observations. It formulates Gaussian initial, transition, and emission distributions and explains why Gaussian closure enables efficient sum-product inference. It develops Kalman filtering and Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing, including their updates, interpretations, tracking application, and posterior quantities needed for EM. It then derives EM parameter-learning updates and notes MAP and Bayesian approaches. Finally, it discusses extensions involving mixture, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and switching models, approximate and variational inference, and particle filtering for sequential Monte Carlo inference.

nodes.title: 13.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text derives the particle filter's predictive distribution as a weighted mixture using Bayes' theorem and graph-based conditional independences, explains sampling and reweighting in the sequential Monte Carlo algorithm, lists its alternative names, and describes the accompanying illustration. It then presents exercises on verifying Markov conditional independences using d-separation or probability rules, demonstrating that state-space observations generally lack a finite-order Markov property, and learning parametric emission parameters by maximum likelihood.

nodes.title: 13.4 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents a schematic particle-filter operation and then lists exercises on Markov and state-space conditional independencies, d-separation, maximum-likelihood learning of parametric HMM emissions, EM derivations for initial, transition, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli parameters, preservation of zero parameters, posterior derivation via factor-graph sum-product messages, and EM training on multiple independent sequences.

nodes.title: 13.8 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on deriving and validating HMM EM-algorithm updates, including constrained maximization for initial and transition probabilities, persistence of zero parameters, Gaussian and discrete/Bernoulli emission updates, and training with multiple independent sequences. It also covers verifying HMM conditional independencies through d-separation and probability rules, and deriving pairwise latent-state posteriors from factor-graph sum-product messages.

nodes.title: 13.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 13.5–13.16 develop and verify key hidden Markov model inference and learning results. They derive EM updates for initial, transition, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emission parameters; examine preservation of zero parameters; verify conditional independences through d-separation and probability rules; derive pairwise latent posteriors using factor-graph message passing; extend EM to multiple independent sequences; connect factor-graph alpha and beta messages with the forward-backward recursions; obtain rescaled marginal formulas; and start the direct derivation of the Viterbi recursion.

nodes.title: 13.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents multi-sequence Baum–Welch parameter re-estimation formulas, including Gaussian emission means, followed by exercises covering equivalence of factor-graph and HMM message definitions, scaled HMM marginals, Viterbi recursion, input-output HMM factorization and inference, Gaussian arguments for latent-state sequence maximization, derivations of Kalman filtering and smoothing identities, augmentation of linear dynamical systems with constant offsets, and the reduction of Kalman filtering for independent observations to Gaussian mean maximum likelihood. The final exercise is truncated after introducing the independent-observation mean-estimation problem.

nodes.title: 13.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sequential data covering initialization of a recursion, factor-graph and forward-backward formulations for input-output hidden Markov models, equivalence between pointwise posterior maximization and most-probable latent sequences in linear dynamical systems, derivations of Kalman filtering and smoothing identities using Gaussian and matrix results, incorporation of constant offsets through state and matrix augmentation, and the reduction of Kalman filtering to maximum-likelihood estimation of a Gaussian mean from independent observations.

nodes.title: 13.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: This excerpt presents Exercises 13.17–13.34 on sequential data and linear dynamical systems. The problems cover factor-graph representations and forward-backward recursions for input-output hidden Markov models; Gaussian posterior modes and Kalman filtering identities; derivation of filtering, smoothing, and Kalman gain equations; affine extensions of state-space models; connections between Kalman filtering, independent Gaussian mean estimation, probabilistic PCA, noiseless state estimation, and averaging for constant states; derivation of RTS smoothing and pairwise posterior covariances; and verification of EM M-step updates for initial, transition, and observation parameters.

This section introduces probabilistic modeling of sequential rather than i.i.d. data, focusing on stationary processes, finite-memory Markov assumptions, and latent-state space models. It develops hidden Markov models, including their structure, inference by forward-backward message passing, EM learning, prediction, scaling, Viterbi decoding, and numerous practical extensions. It then treats linear dynamical systems as continuous linear-Gaussian state-space models, deriving Kalman filtering, Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing, EM learning, and related MAP, Bayesian, nonlinear, switching, mixture, variational, and particle-filter methods. The accompanying exercises reinforce conditional-independence reasoning, HMM inference and parameter estimation, multi-sequence training, message-passing and decoding equivalences, input-output models, particle filtering, and the derivation and applications of Kalman filtering and smoothing.

nodes.title: 14 Combining Models
14.1. Bayesian Model Averaging
nodes.summary: The text introduces model combination through input-dependent selection, emphasizing decision trees, their hard splits, and softened probabilistic mixtures of experts. It distinguishes model combination from Bayesian model averaging: mixtures allow different data points to come from different components, whereas Bayesian averaging assumes one model generated the entire data set and averages uncertainty over candidate models. It then introduces committees as prediction-averaging ensembles, motivated by reducing the bias–variance trade-off, before beginning a discussion of bias and variance.

nodes.title: 14.2. Committees
nodes.summary: The text distinguishes model combination from Bayesian model averaging, explaining that combination can assign different latent components to different observations, whereas model averaging assumes one model generates the entire data set and updates uncertainty over that model. It then introduces committees that average predictions to reduce variance, describes bootstrap aggregation (bagging), derives its error reduction under zero-mean uncorrelated model errors, and notes the practical limitation of correlated errors. Finally, it introduces boosting and AdaBoost, which train weak binary classifiers sequentially on reweighted data that emphasizes previous mistakes and combine them through weighted voting, with possible extension to regression.

nodes.title: 14.3. Boosting
14.3.1 Minimizing exponential error
nodes.summary: The text completes the AdaBoost prediction rule and explains how iterative weighting emphasizes misclassified examples while assigning larger ensemble coefficients to more accurate base learners. It describes the decision-stump illustration and then derives AdaBoost as sequential minimization of an exponential error: fixing earlier learners, minimizing over the next learner reproduces weighted-error training, minimizing over its coefficient gives the AdaBoost coefficient, and the resulting exponential update reduces to the standard weight rule. Final prediction is the sign of the combined classifier. It concludes by examining the expected exponential loss and showing that unrestricted functional minimization yields half the log conditional-probability odds.

nodes.title: 14.3.2 Error functions for boosting
nodes.summary: The text completes the derivation of AdaBoost’s exponential-loss minimization, including base-classifier selection, coefficient determination, data-weight updates, and final sign-based classification. It explains that exponential-loss minimization estimates half the log-odds, compares exponential, cross-entropy, hinge, and misclassification losses, and discusses exponential loss’s simplicity, lack of probabilistic and multiclass interpretations, and sensitivity to outliers. It then extends boosting ideas to regression using squared or more robust absolute loss, illustrated by error-function comparisons, before introducing tree-based models, their axis-aligned recursive partitions and binary-tree interpretation, and the CART, ID3, and C4.5 frameworks.

This section introduces boosting as a more powerful alternative to simple committee averaging, focusing on AdaBoost's sequential training, adaptive example weighting, classifier weighting, and weighted-vote prediction. It derives the method through exponential-loss minimization, relates the loss to conditional log-odds, compares it with other classification losses, and discusses its limitations. The section also covers regression extensions using alternative losses and introduces decision-tree models and major tree-learning frameworks used with boosting.

nodes.title: 14.4. Tree-based Models
nodes.summary: The text contrasts robust absolute-deviation boosting with squared-error boosting, then explains CART tree-based models: recursive axis-aligned binary partitioning, interpretable traversal and leaf predictions, regression fitting by regional means, greedy split selection, and complexity-controlled pruning. It gives the regression pruning objective and the classification alternatives of cross-entropy and Gini index, explaining their properties and use in growth versus pruning. It concludes with the instability and representational limitations of conventional hard, axis-aligned trees and motivates soft, probabilistic conditional mixture models and hierarchical mixtures of experts.

nodes.title: 14.5. Conditional Mixture Models
14.5.1 Mixtures of linear regression models
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional mixture models and develops mixtures of linear regression models using EM. It defines the model and likelihood, adds latent component assignments, derives responsibility calculations in the E-step, and obtains M-step updates for mixing coefficients, component regression weights via weighted least squares, and the shared noise precision. A two-line synthetic example illustrates convergence, responsibilities, improved likelihood over single regression, and the limitation of input-independent mixture weights. The text then begins mixtures of logistic regression models, defining their Bernoulli-logistic component density and parameters, with the likelihood derivation left incomplete in the excerpt.

nodes.title: 14.5.2 Mixtures of logistic models
nodes.summary: The text presents examples and theory for combining predictive models. It first illustrates EM training of a two-component linear regression mixture and compares its substantially improved bimodal predictive density with a single linear regression. It then develops mixtures of logistic regression models, giving their conditional and complete-data likelihoods, EM responsibilities, expected log likelihood, mixing-coefficient update, and component gradients and Hessians. The component updates reduce to independently fitting weighted logistic regressions, typically with IRLS, and the approach extends to softmax mixtures. Finally, it introduces mixtures of experts, in which input-dependent gating functions determine the mixing coefficients while specialized expert models describe different regions of input space.

nodes.title: 14.5.3 Mixtures of experts
nodes.summary: The text completes the EM treatment of mixtures of logistic regressions, deriving the mixing-coefficient update and showing that each component is independently fitted as a responsibility-weighted logistic regression using IRLS, with an illustrative comparison to a single classifier and an extension to softmax mixtures. It then introduces mixtures of experts, in which input-dependent gating functions select among expert conditional distributions, and discusses linear gating and experts, hierarchical mixtures of experts as probabilistic decision trees, EM/IRLS training, Bayesian treatment, and the relationship with mixture density networks. The included exercises cover Bayesian predictive averaging and latent-variable marginalization, committee-error derivations, Jensen-inequality bounds for convex losses, and the conditions under which a weighted committee prediction lies between its members’ minimum and maximum predictions.

The section reviews the strengths and limitations of standard decision trees, including impurity measures, instability, axis-aligned hard splits, and discontinuous predictions, then develops conditional mixture models as a probabilistic alternative. It covers EM training for mixtures of linear and logistic regression models, including responsibilities, likelihoods, weighted least-squares or IRLS component updates, mixing coefficients, precision, examples, and softmax extensions. It then introduces mixtures of experts with input-dependent gating, hierarchical probabilistic trees, Bayesian and mixture-density-network connections, and concludes with exercises on Bayesian averaging, committee errors, convex-loss bounds, and weighted predictions.

nodes.title: 14.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text notes that mixture density networks use shared hidden units for component densities and mixing coefficients, allowing soft, non-axis-aligned, nonlinear input-space partitions unlike hierarchical mixtures of experts. It then presents exercises on marginalizing model indices and latent variables in predictive distributions, distinguishing Bayesian model averaging from within-model latent variables; deriving committee-error relationships; proving via Jensen’s inequality that a committee’s expected error is no greater than the average member error; extending this result to arbitrary convex error functions; and establishing that a weighted committee prediction remains between the members’ minimum and maximum exactly when its weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

nodes.title: 14.3 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text notes that mixture density networks provide flexible, nonlinear soft partitions of input space. It then presents exercises on marginalizing latent variables and model indices in Bayesian predictive distributions, contrasting model averaging with latent variables within one model; deriving committee-error relations; proving via Jensen's inequality that a committee is no worse than its average members for squared or any convex error; and establishing that bounded, convex-combination committee predictions require nonnegative weights summing to one.

nodes.title: 14.5 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of combining models by comparing mixture density networks with hierarchical mixtures of experts, emphasizing their flexible nonlinear, non-axis-aligned soft partitions. It then presents exercises on marginalizing latent variables and model uncertainty in Bayesian prediction, deriving committee error relationships, proving via Jensen’s inequality that averaging predictions cannot increase convex error, extending this result to all convex error functions, and characterizing valid nonnegative normalized weights for unequal committee members.

nodes.title: 14.6 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 14.6–14.15 ask for derivations and verifications concerning AdaBoost, exponential-error minimization, residual fitting in squared-error boosting, and decision-tree impurity measures. They also address extensions and maximum-likelihood EM estimation for mixtures of linear regression models, including vector targets, complete-data likelihoods, mixing-coefficient updates, and conditional-mean predictions, with a warning about poor mean predictions for multimodal distributions.

nodes.title: 14.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 14.6–14.15 cover derivations and checks involving AdaBoost, including the coefficient update, variational minimization of exponential error, and the lack of a properly normalized probabilistic interpretation; boosting with squared-error residuals; the mean as the optimal constant least-squares prediction; comparison of tree misclassification, cross-entropy, and Gini criteria; extensions of mixture linear regression to vector targets; verification of its complete-data likelihood; derivation of mixing-coefficient updates by Lagrange multipliers; and derivation and limitations of the mixture model’s conditional-mean prediction.

nodes.title: 14.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 14.6–14.15 cover derivations and verifications concerning AdaBoost error minimization and parameter updates, variational minimization of exponential loss, the lack of a corresponding normalized probabilistic model, boosting with squared-error residuals, and the mean as the optimal constant squared-error predictor. They also compare tree impurity measures using misclassification rate, cross-entropy, and the Gini index; extend mixture-of-linear-regression results to vector targets; verify the complete-data likelihood; derive EM mixing-coefficient updates using Lagrange multipliers; and derive and interpret the conditional mean prediction for mixtures of linear regressions, particularly for multimodal distributions.

nodes.title: 14.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 14.6–14.17 address derivations and properties of boosting, including the AdaBoost coefficient update, variational minimization of exponential loss, the lack of a corresponding normalized probabilistic model, residual fitting under squared loss, and the mean as the optimal constant prediction. They compare classification-tree impurity measures, extend mixtures of linear regressions to vector targets, derive their complete-data likelihood and EM mixing-coefficient update, analyze conditional-mean predictions, formulate EM for mixtures of softmax classifiers, and investigate when hierarchical mixtures can or cannot be reduced to single-level mixtures, especially under linear logistic or softmax gating functions.

nodes.title: 14.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents two exercises on mixture models: deriving EM for a mixture of softmax classifiers, and analyzing hierarchical conditional mixtures. Hierarchical mixtures collapse to ordinary mixtures when component and mixing functions are unrestricted, including x-dependent coefficients, but generally do not collapse to a single-level mixture when both levels are constrained to linear logistic or softmax gating models; a two-level two-plus-two-component counterexample is suggested.

This section surveys ensemble and mixture methods for combining models. It contrasts Bayesian model averaging with mixtures that assign different observations to different components, explains committees and bagging as variance-reduction methods, and develops boosting and AdaBoost through sequential reweighting, weighted voting, exponential-loss minimization, classification-loss comparisons, limitations, and regression extensions. It then presents CART trees, including their construction, prediction rules, split criteria, pruning, and weaknesses, motivating conditional mixtures and hierarchical mixtures of experts. These probabilistic models are trained with EM and related weighted regression or classification updates, use input-dependent gating, and include mixture-density networks capable of flexible nonlinear soft partitions. Exercises reinforce Bayesian marginalization, ensemble-error results, convexity bounds, boosting derivations, tree criteria, mixture-regression likelihoods and EM updates, softmax mixtures, conditional means, and hierarchical-mixture equivalence.

Appendix C covers dimensionality reduction and latent-variable modeling from conventional, probabilistic, factor, kernel, and nonlinear PCA through ICA, neural, manifold, and related models, including their derivations, inference, estimation, Bayesian extensions, computational issues, applications, and extensive exercises. It then addresses sequential probabilistic data through HMMs and linear dynamical systems, with filtering, smoothing, decoding, learning, and nonlinear or approximate extensions. Finally, it surveys model-combination techniques such as Bayesian averaging, mixtures, bagging, boosting, decision trees, mixtures of experts, and mixture-density networks, including their objectives, training algorithms, limitations, and exercises.

structure.summary: This section provides a broad treatment of machine learning and probabilistic modeling, beginning with learning paradigms, regression, decision theory, information theory, probability distributions, likelihood, Bayesian inference, model selection, and dimensionality control. It develops a wide range of distributions and inference techniques, including maximum-likelihood, conjugate, variational, expectation-propagation, Monte Carlo, and graphical-model methods. It further covers regression, classification, neural and kernel methods, Gaussian processes, mixture and latent-variable models, dimensionality reduction, ICA, manifold learning, HMMs, dynamical systems, and model-combination techniques, with derivations, computational methods, uncertainty analysis, applications, and extensive exercises. The contents conclude with appendices on calculus of variations and Lagrange multipliers, references, and an index.

structure.title: Appendix A. Data Sets

nodes.title: Handwritten Digits
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces the book’s data sets and directs readers to the book website for files and format details. It describes MNIST handwritten digits, including their NIST origin, training and test sizes, contributor separation, image preprocessing, example figure, and benchmark classification error rates. It also introduces the synthetic Oil Flow data set, explaining dual-energy gamma densitometry, why two beam energies are needed to estimate the three phase proportions, and the complication of low-velocity laminar or stratified flow in which water, oil, and gas form layers.

nodes.title: Oil Flow
nodes.summary: The text introduces a figure of randomly selected MNIST digits, then describes the synthetic Oil Flow data set, which uses noisy measurements from six dual-energy gamma beams to infer oil, water, and gas fractions and one of three flow geometries. It explains the physical basis, data-generation procedure, sample contents, data splits, applications, and the linear, nonlinear, segmented, and intersecting manifold structure of the observations. It also presents the 272-observation Old Faithful data set, recording eruption duration and time to the next eruption, whose variables show useful predictive dependence.

nodes.title: Old Faithful
nodes.summary: The text describes manifold structure in oil-and-water observations for homogeneous, annular, and laminar phase configurations, including noise, nonlinearities, discontinuities, segmentation, and intersections. It then introduces the 272-observation Old Faithful eruption data set and its predictive relationship between eruption duration and waiting time, followed by two synthetic data sets used throughout the book: noisy sinusoidal regression and a two-class Gaussian-mixture classification problem with analytically accessible posteriors and decision boundary.

nodes.title: Synthetic Data
nodes.summary: The text describes the Old Faithful plot and two synthetic data sets used throughout the book: a noisy sinusoidal regression set and a two-class Gaussian-based classification set. It explains how each is generated and notes that the accompanying figures display the regression function and conditional distribution, as well as classification posterior probabilities and the optimal 0.5-posterior decision boundary.

structure.summary: Appendix A introduces the book’s data sets and website resources, covering MNIST digits and their origin, organization, preprocessing, and benchmark results; the synthetic Oil Flow data, its gamma-densitometry basis, phase and geometry inference, generation, applications, and complex manifold structure; the Old Faithful eruption data and its predictive variables; and synthetic sinusoidal-regression and Gaussian-mixture-classification examples, including their generation, conditional distributions, posterior probabilities, and optimal decision boundary.

structure.title: Appendix B. Probability Distributions

nodes.title: Bernoulli
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces its purpose of summarizing common exponential-family probability distributions and their main statistics. It then presents the Bernoulli distribution for a binary variable, giving its parameterization, probability mass function, expectation, variance, mode, and entropy, and noting its relationship to the binomial distribution and its beta conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Beta
nodes.summary: The text defines the beta and binomial probability distributions, giving their parameters, formulas, moments, modes, interpretations, and key relationships. The beta distribution models probabilities on [0,1], is conjugate to the Bernoulli distribution, includes the uniform distribution as a special case, and is a two-state Dirichlet distribution. The binomial distribution models the number of successes in N Bernoulli trials, explains its combinatorial coefficient and factorial notation, identifies the Bernoulli and Gaussian special or limiting cases, and states that the beta distribution is its conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Binomial
nodes.summary: The text introduces the beta, binomial, and Dirichlet probability distributions, giving their definitions, parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, and key properties. It explains beta–Bernoulli and Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy, interprets their parameters as effective observation counts, defines binomial coefficients and factorials, notes special cases and Gaussian approximation, and provides the Dirichlet normalization constant, digamma-based log moments, entropy, covariance structure, and density conditions.

nodes.title: Gamma
nodes.summary: The text presents the Gamma and Gaussian probability distributions, including their parameters, densities, moments, modes, expected log value, and entropy. It explains Gamma–Gaussian conjugacy for precision and mean parameters, identifies the exponential distribution as the a = 1 Gamma case, defines precision and standard deviation, and introduces the multivariate Gaussian through its mean vector and symmetric covariance matrix.

nodes.title: Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text surveys Gamma, univariate and multivariate Gaussian, Gaussian-Gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, and Multinomial probability distributions. It presents their parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, entropies, conjugate-prior relationships, and key Gaussian properties, including marginalization, conditioning, linear transformations, Gaussian propagation, and partitioned conditional formulas. It concludes by defining the multinomial distribution and listing its basic statistics and entropy.

nodes.title: Gaussian-Gamma
nodes.summary: The text presents a Gaussian marginal, conjugate Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart priors for unknown Gaussian parameters, notes their scalar equivalence, and introduces the one-hot multinomial distribution along with its probability mass function, means, variances, covariances, and entropy.

nodes.title: Gaussian-Wishart
nodes.summary: The text presents the Gaussian marginal distribution, defines Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors for unknown Gaussian means and precisions, notes their scalar equivalence, and introduces the one-hot multinomial distribution along with its probability, moments, covariance, and entropy.

nodes.title: Multinomial
nodes.summary: The text reviews Gaussian marginalization and several standard probability distributions and conjugate priors. It defines the Gaussian-Gamma prior for an unknown univariate Gaussian mean and precision, the Gaussian-Wishart prior for unknown multivariate mean and precision, and notes their scalar equivalence. It then introduces one-hot multinomial variables and multinomial count distributions, giving their constraints, probabilities, moments, covariances, entropy, combinatorial coefficient, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It clarifies the terminology linking normal and Gaussian distributions and begins describing the Student’s t-distribution as a Gaussian with Gamma-distributed precision integrated out.

nodes.title: Normal
nodes.summary: The text defines the multinomial distribution, its probability formula, parameter constraints, combinatorial coefficient, moments, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It also clarifies the book’s terminology equating normal with Gaussian and renaming related distributions, then introduces the historical origin and Gaussian-gamma mixture construction of Student’s t-distribution.

nodes.title: Student’s t
nodes.summary: The text presents the multinomial distribution, including its constraints, probability mass function, combinatorial interpretation, moments, covariances, and Dirichlet conjugate prior; clarifies terminology equating the normal distribution with the Gaussian; and describes univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, their Bayesian derivations, parameters, moments, special Cauchy case, Gaussian limit, and robustness. It concludes with the uniform distribution’s density, moments, entropy, and affine transformation property.

nodes.title: Uniform
nodes.summary: The text covers the univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, including their densities, moments, mode, degrees of freedom, Cauchy special case, Mahalanobis-distance form, Gaussian limiting behavior, Wishart-mixture interpretation, and robustness to outliers. It then introduces the continuous uniform distribution, specifying its support, density, mean, variance, entropy, and transformation from a standard uniform variable.

nodes.title: Von Mises
nodes.summary: The text defines the von Mises circular Gaussian distribution, its density, periodicity, interpretation, parameters, and Gaussian approximation. It then presents the Wishart distribution as the conjugate prior for a multivariate Gaussian precision matrix, giving its density, normalization constant, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter restrictions, and its reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

nodes.title: Wishart
nodes.summary: The text introduces the von Mises circular Gaussian distribution, giving its periodic density, Bessel-function normalization, interpretation of its location and concentration parameters, origin-dependence of expectations, and Gaussian approximation for high concentration. It then presents the Wishart distribution as the multivariate Gaussian precision-matrix conjugate prior, including its density and normalization, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, matrix and parameter conditions, and its reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

structure.summary: This appendix surveys common probability distributions and their main statistics, formulas, parameter constraints, special cases, approximations, and conjugate relationships. It covers Bernoulli, beta, binomial, Dirichlet, Gamma, Gaussian and related Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart models, multinomial, Student's t, uniform, von Mises, and Wishart distributions. It also explains Gaussian marginalization, conditioning, transformations, and propagation; interprets conjugate parameters as effective counts where applicable; describes categorical and combinatorial constructions; and connects distributions through special cases, mixtures, limiting behavior, and Bayesian conjugacy.

structure.title: Appendix C. Properties of Matrices

nodes.title: Basic Matrix Identities
nodes.summary: The appendix reviews foundational matrix notation and identities, including transpose and inverse rules, computationally useful inverse formulas, the special inverse identity, and the Woodbury identity. It defines linear independence and matrix rank, then introduces trace and determinant, giving cyclic trace properties and the determinant’s signed permutation-sum definition. The presentation assumes basic linear algebra, notes proof methods and computational advantages, and cites standard references for further study.

nodes.title: Traces and Determinants
nodes.summary: The text develops matrix identities for inverses, including a computationally useful reformulation, a special inverse identity, and the Woodbury identity; defines linear independence and matrix rank; explains trace properties and determinant definitions and identities; and introduces componentwise derivatives of vectors and matrices, including the derivative of a linear scalar product.

nodes.title: Matrix Derivatives
nodes.summary: The text presents determinant definitions and identities, including the 2 × 2 formula, product and inverse rules, Sylvester’s theorem, and the matrix determinant lemma. It then introduces vector and matrix derivatives and lists fundamental matrix-calculus identities for scalar products, products, inverses, determinants, and traces. Finally, it defines the eigenvector equation Au_i = λ_i u_i for square matrices.

nodes.title: Eigenvector Equation
nodes.summary: The text presents key matrix derivative rules for products, inverses, determinants, and traces, then develops the eigenvalue equation and characteristic polynomial. It focuses on symmetric matrices, showing that their inverses are symmetric, eigenvalues are real, and eigenvectors can be chosen as an orthonormal complete basis. These eigenvectors form an orthogonal matrix that preserves lengths and angles and diagonalizes the matrix, yielding spectral expressions for the matrix and its inverse, as well as determinant and trace formulas. Finally, it defines positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices through quadratic forms and eigenvalue signs, emphasizing that positive definiteness does not mean all entries are positive.

structure.summary: This appendix reviews foundational matrix algebra, covering transpose and inverse identities, the Woodbury identity, rank, trace, determinant formulas and theorems, and matrix derivatives. It then develops eigenvalue and eigenvector theory, especially for symmetric matrices, including orthonormal diagonalization, spectral expressions, determinant and trace results, and the characterization of positive definite and semidefinite matrices through quadratic forms and eigenvalues.

structure.title: Appendix D. Calculus of Variations
structure.summary: The appendix introduces the calculus of variations as the optimization of functionals over functions, relating it to ordinary derivatives through arbitrary function perturbations. It defines functional derivatives, shows why stationarity requires them to vanish, and derives the Euler–Lagrange equation for integral functionals depending on a function, its derivative, and position. An example produces a second-order differential equation solved with boundary conditions. It also covers the simpler case without derivative dependence, normalization constraints for probability distributions via Lagrange multipliers, multidimensional extensions, and applications such as shortest paths and maximum entropy.

structure.title: Appendix E. Lagrange Multipliers
structure.summary: The appendix develops Lagrange multipliers geometrically and algebraically for optimizing multivariable functions under equality and inequality constraints. It explains why constraint and objective gradients align at a constrained stationary point, defines the Lagrangian and its stationarity equations, works through a two-variable example, introduces the KKT conditions and sign conventions for inequalities and minimization, and extends the formulation to multiple equality and inequality constraints and constrained functional derivatives.
